src.name: Shipping a prompt is a deploy
src.desc: Prompts are code and need versioning, review and rollback
src.what:
Prompts live in the repo, change through pull requests, carry versions, and are recorded per request in traces. Model version is pinned explicitly. Rolling back a prompt is as available as rolling back code.

🧠 Analogy: a database migration. Nobody edits production schema in a web console, and for the same reasons.
src.analogy:
A prompt management dashboard let anyone edit production prompts in a browser. Convenient, and a marketing colleague adjusted the tone guidance one afternoon.

Quality dropped. There was no diff, no author, no timestamp, no previous version, and no way to roll back — the old text simply no longer existed anywhere. It took two days to reconstruct approximately what had been there before, from memory.

Prompts in the repo, changed through pull requests, version stamped into every trace. A prompt edited in a console is an unreviewed production deploy with no rollback.
src.why:
A prompt edited in a dashboard is an unreviewed production deploy with no rollback. A one-word change can move quality several percent and nobody will know which word.

Kaise karna hai:

Prompts in the repo, eval gate on the pull request, prompt version stamped into every trace.
gotchas: Pin the model version explicitly. A stable alias can point at new weights without warning.
Record the prompt version in the trace, or you cannot tell which version produced an old bad answer.
A prompt management dashboard without version control and review is a liability, however convenient.

src.name: Tooling ke saath — kya milta hai, kya jaata hai
src.desc: Vite/esbuild add karo aur imaandari se dono taraf ka hisaab likho.
src.what: Ek bundler (Vite, esbuild, webpack) teen kaam karta hai: transform (JSX → JS), bundle (50 file → 1 file), aur dev server (HMR, fast reload).
src.why:
Kya milta hai: JSX ka aaram; ek network request; minify + tree-shaking se chhota bundle; HMR jisse state bachte hue code reload hota hai; node_modules se import (bina URL likhe); TypeScript, CSS modules, images — sab.

Kya jaata hai: ab tumhara code aur browser ka code alag hain — debugging ke liye source maps chahiye; ek aur config file jo tootegi; node_modules mein 200MB; build time; aur sabse badi baat — ek aur cheez jo tumhe samajhni padegi.

Kaise karna hai:

Ye faisla mechanical nahi, situational hai. Chhota learning project, ek-do file, sikhne ke liye → zero tooling behtar hai, kyunki tum wahi dekh rahe ho jo chal raha hai. Bada app, team, TypeScript, 50+ files → tooling ki keemat wasool ho jaati hai.

Interview mein ye sawaal aata hai. Sahi jawab "Vite use karo" nahi hai — sahi jawab hai "ye kis cheez ke badle kya de raha hai, aur mere case mein kya zyada keemti hai".
src.code:
# EK HI APP, DO BAAR. Do folder banao.

# ---- A) zero tooling ----
# app-plain/index.html + app.js, sirf h() calls
python3 -m http.server 8080
# naapo: pehla paint kitne ms mein, kitni network requests, total KB

# ---- B) vite + jsx ----
npm create vite@latest app-jsx -- --template vanilla
cd app-jsx && npm i

# vite.config.js
export default {
  esbuild: { jsxFactory: "h", jsxFragment: "Fragment" }
};

npm run dev     # HMR try karo -- counter badhao, code edit karo, count bacha?
npm run build   # dist/ ka size dekho

# HISAAB TABLE README mein likho:
# | metric              | zero tooling | vite+jsx |
# | setup time          |              |          |
# | node_modules size   |     0 MB     |          |
# | dev first paint     |              |          |
# | prod bundle KB      |              |          |
# | JSX?                |     nahi     |    haan  |
# | HMR (state bachta)? |     nahi     |    haan  |
# | debug: jo likha wahi chal raha? | haan | source map se |
gotchas: jsxFactory set karna bhool gaye to esbuild "React is not defined" dega — kyunki default factory React.createElement hai.
HMR ko "reload" mat samjho. Reload state uda deta hai, HMR sirf badla hua module badalta hai aur state bacha leta hai. Ye asli productivity ka farak hai.
Bundle size ko production build se naapo, dev se nahi. Dev bundle jaan-boojh kar bada aur unminified hota hai.

en.name: With tooling — what you get, what you lose
en.desc: Add Vite/esbuild and honestly write the accounting on both sides.
en.what: A bundler (Vite, esbuild, webpack) does three things: transform (JSX → JS), bundle (50 file → 1 file), and dev server (HMR, fast reload).
en.why:
What you get: the convenience of JSX; a single network request; a smaller bundle thanks to minify + tree‑shaking; HMR that reloads code while preserving state; imports from node_modules (without writing URLs); TypeScript, CSS modules, images — everything.

What you lose: your code and the browser’s code are now separate — you need source maps for debugging; an extra config file that can break; node_modules taking up 200 MB; build time; and the biggest point — one more thing you’ll have to understand.
gotchas: If you forget to set jsxFactory, esbuild will give "React is not defined" — because the default factory is React.createElement.
Don’t treat HMR as a "reload". Reload discards state, while HMR only replaces the changed module and preserves state. This is the real productivity difference.
Measure bundle size from a production build, not from dev. The dev bundle is intentionally larger and unminified.
en.visualCap: Two paths, one destination. Tooling doesn’t unlock a feature — it only provides convenience and, in return, adds a layer of indirection.

src.name: Work loop — pause aur resume
src.desc: Ek variable mein poori position. Ruko, browser ko do, wapas wahin se shuru.
src.what:
Ab dekho ki magic kya hai: nextUnitOfWork ek variable hai jisme hamari poori position hai. Loop ruk sakta hai, function return kar sakta hai, browser jo chahe kar sakta hai — aur jab wapas aayenge, us variable se kaam wahin se chalu ho jaayega.

Isko resumable computation kehte hain. Aur ye Fiber ka poora point hai — baaki sab (priority, suspense, concurrent) isi ek property ke upar bana hai.
src.why:
Ek baar tumhare paas resumable work ho, to bahut kuch mumkin ho jaata hai:

• Beech mein zyada zaroori kaam aa jaaye to usko pehle karo (priority)
• Kaam phenk do agar wo purana ho gaya (user ne aur type kar diya)
• Ek kaam ko rok ke rakho jab tak data na aaye (Suspense)

Hum in mein se koi nahi banayenge — par ab tum bata sakte ho ki ye kaise mumkin hain. Aur interview mein wahi puchha jaata hai.

Kaise karna hai:

Ek chhota par zaroori detail: hum wipRoot (work in progress root) rakhte hain, aur currentRoot (jo abhi screen pe hai). Kaam wipRoot pe hota hai, screen currentRoot dikhati hai.

Ye do alag trees hona hi Phase 12 ki neev hai. Aur ye ek jaana-pehchana pattern hai — graphics mein isko double buffering kehte hain: ek buffer pe likho, dusra dikhao, phir swap kar do.
gotchas: Agar pause 0 aaye to matlab tumhara tree itna chhota hai ki ek idle period mein khatam ho gaya. 10000+ nodes lo, aur CPU throttling lagao.
requestIdleCallback ka deadline browser ke mood pe depend karta hai. Kabhi 50ms milega, kabhi 1ms. Ye normal hai — code dono handle kare.
console.log ko har unit pe mat lagao — wo khud itna slow hai ki measurement bekaar ho jaayega.

en.name: Work loop — pause and resume
en.desc: The entire position is stored in a variable. Pause, give control to the browser, then resume from the same spot.
en.what:
Now see the magic: nextUnitOfWork is a variable that holds our entire position. The loop can pause, the function can return, the browser can do whatever — and when we come back, work will resume from that variable.

This is called resumable computation. It is the whole point of Fibers — everything else (priority, suspense, concurrent) is built on this single property.
en.why:
Once you have resumable work, many things become possible:

• If a more important task arrives, handle it first (priority)
• Discard work if it becomes stale (the user typed more)
• Pause a task until data arrives (Suspense)

We won't implement any of these now — but you should be able to explain how they are possible. That's what interviewers ask.

How to do it:

A small but important detail: we keep a wipRoot (work‑in‑progress root) and a currentRoot (the one currently on screen). Work happens on wipRoot, the screen shows currentRoot.

Having two separate trees is the foundation of Phase 12. This is a well‑known pattern — in graphics it is called double buffering: write to one buffer, display the other, then swap.
gotchas: If pause is 0, it means your tree is so small that it finishes within a single idle period. Try with 10,000+ nodes and apply CPU throttling.
The deadline for requestIdleCallback depends on the browser's state. Sometimes you get 50 ms, sometimes 1 ms. This is normal — the code should handle both.
Don't place console.log on every unit — it is slow enough to ruin measurements.

src.name: Four Conditions for Deadlock
src.desc: Coffman conditions: Mutual Exclusion, Hold & Wait, No Preemption, Circular Wait. All 4 must hold.
src.q: What are the four necessary conditions for deadlock? To prevent deadlock, which one would you eliminate?
src.qsub: Draw a resource allocation graph and show how it demonstrates a deadlock.
src.what:
Definition: Deadlock tab hota hai jab Coffman ki chaaron conditions ek saath hon. Inme se ek bhi tod do to deadlock nahi ho sakta.

Classic: Thread 1 ne lock A liya, B maanga; Thread 2 ne B liya, A maanga.
src.analogy: Chaurahe par chaaron taraf se gaadiyan fans gayi — koi peeche nahi hat sakta, sab agle ka wait kar rahe hain.
src.why: Chaaron yaad rakhne se prevention strategy turant samajh aati hai: har condition ek tarah ka fix suggest karti hai.
where: Dono taraf se lock lene wale.
cons: Runtime par rare aur reproduce karna mushkil
gotchas: Chaaron conditions hone chahiye — ek todo, solve
Database deadlock detection ke baad ek transaction abort karta hai
Thread dump (jstack) se cycle dikhta hai

en.name: Four Conditions for Deadlock
en.desc: Coffman conditions: Mutual Exclusion, Hold & Wait, No Preemption, Circular Wait. All 4 must hold.
en.q: What are the four necessary conditions for deadlock? To prevent deadlock, which one would you eliminate?
en.qsub: Draw a resource allocation graph and show how it demonstrates a deadlock.
en.what:
Definition: A deadlock occurs when all four Coffman conditions hold simultaneously. Breaking any one prevents a deadlock.

Classic example: Thread 1 holds lock A and requests B; Thread 2 holds B and requests A.
en.analogy: At an intersection, cars come from all four directions — none can move backward, each waits for the next.
en.why: Remembering the four helps quickly devise a prevention strategy: each condition suggests a type of fix.
cons: Runtime par rare aur reproduce karna mushkil
gotchas: All four conditions must be present — break one to solve
After detecting a database deadlock, a transaction is aborted
A thread dump (jstack) shows the cycle
terms: Holding one resource while requesting another.
where: Dono taraf se lock lene wale.

src.name: Futures, Promises & Async/Await
src.desc: A Future represents a value not yet computed. Promise resolves it later. Async/await is syntactic sugar over Futures.
src.q: What is the difference between a Future and a Promise? How does CompletableFuture in Java work?
src.qsub: What is structured concurrency? How does it improve on raw threads and futures?
terms: Abhi na mili value ka placeholder.
Value set karne wala writable side.
src.what: Definition: Future ek pending result hai jo baad mein resolve ya reject hota hai. async/await compiler/runtime state machine banata hai jo await par thread chhod deta hai (block nahi karta).
src.why: Callback hell ke bina asynchronous kaam compose karna (chain, all, race) aur errors ek jagah handle karna.
cons: Error handling aur cancellation subtle
Sequential await galti se serial ho jaata hai
gotchas: await loop mein serial hota hai — Promise.all use karo
Future.get() blocking hai
Unhandled rejection process crash kar sakta hai

en.name: Futures, Promises & Async/Await
en.desc: A Future represents a value not yet computed. Promise resolves it later. Async/await is syntactic sugar over Futures.
en.q: What is the difference between a Future and a Promise? How does CompletableFuture in Java work?
en.qsub: What is structured concurrency? How does it improve on raw threads and futures?
en.what: Definition: A Future is a pending result that is resolved or rejected later. async/await creates a compiler/runtime state machine that releases the thread at await (does not block).
en.why: Compose asynchronous work (chain, all, race) and handle errors in one place without callback hell.
cons: Error handling aur cancellation subtle
Sequential await galti se serial ho jaata hai
gotchas: await loop runs serially — use Promise.all
Future.get() blocks
An unhandled rejection can crash the process
terms: Placeholder for a value that has not yet arrived.
Writable side that sets the value.

src.name: Media Queries
src.desc: min-width/max-width breakpoints, feature queries, orientation, prefers-color-scheme / reduced-motion.
src.q: How do media queries work? What does prefers-reduced-motion let you do?
src.qsub: What is the difference between min-width and max-width breakpoint strategies?
terms: Viewport width jis par layout badalta hai — content decide kare, device nahi.
Browser support check — media query nahi, feature query.
src.what:
Definition: @media conditional CSS hai: viewport width (min-width/max-width), orientation, aur user preferences (dark mode, reduced motion, contrast) ke hisaab se rules lagate hain.

Modern syntax: @media (400px <= width <= 900px).
src.why: Responsive design ka base. User preference queries (reduced motion, dark mode) accessibility aur polish ke liye zaroori hain — ye sirf screen size ki baat nahi.
pros: User preferences ko respect karna aasan
cons: Viewport-based hai, component-based nahi (container queries isi ka jawab hain)
gotchas: Breakpoints device names par nahi, content ke toot-ne par rakho
max-width aur min-width mix karne se overlap/gaps ho sakte hain
Hover-only interactions touch par kaam nahi karte — (hover: hover) se guard karo

en.name: Media Queries
en.desc: min-width/max-width breakpoints, feature queries, orientation, prefers-color-scheme / reduced-motion.
en.q: How do media queries work? What does prefers-reduced-motion let you do?
en.qsub: What is the difference between min-width and max-width breakpoint strategies?
en.what:
Definition: @media is conditional CSS that applies rules based on viewport width (min-width/max-width), orientation, and user preferences (dark mode, reduced motion, contrast).

Modern syntax: min-width.
en.why: The foundation of responsive design. User preference queries (reduced motion, dark mode) are essential for accessibility and polish — they’re not just about screen size.
pros: User preferences ko respect karna aasan
cons: Viewport-based hai, component-based nahi (container queries isi ka jawab hain)
gotchas: Set breakpoints based on content breaking, not device names
Mixing max-width and min-width can cause overlaps/gaps
Hover‑only interactions don’t work on touch devices — guard them with (hover: hover)
terms: Viewport width at which the layout changes — let the content decide, not the device.
Browser support check — not a media query, a feature query.

src.name: Viewport Units & Mobile Gotchas
src.desc: vw/vh/vmin/vmax, the mobile 100vh address-bar problem, dvh/svh/lvh dynamic units.
src.q: Why does 100vh behave badly on mobile browsers, and how do dvh/svh fix it?
src.qsub: When would you use vmin or vmax?
terms: Small / large / dynamic viewport height — mobile address bar ke hisaab se.
src.what:
Definition: vw/vh viewport relative hain. Mobile par address bar scroll par chhupti-dikhti hai to 100vh ek fixed (large) viewport maanta hai aur content bar ke neeche chhup sakta hai.

Fix: dvh (dynamic, bar ke saath badalta), svh (hamesha safe, chhota), lvh (bar hata kar).
src.why: Full-screen hero ya bottom-fixed button mobile par 'neeche cut ho raha' wala bug iske wajah se aata hai. Modern solution dvh hai.
cons: dvh se layout address-bar scroll par resize ho sakta hai
gotchas: 100vw vertical scrollbar ko include karta hai — horizontal scroll aa sakta hai
dvh animate/resize ke saath jank de sakta hai; svh safer
Purane browsers ke liye vh fallback pehle likho

en.name: Viewport Units & Mobile Gotchas
en.desc: vw/vh/vmin/vmax, the mobile 100vh address-bar problem, dvh/svh/lvh dynamic units.
en.q: Why does 100vh behave badly on mobile browsers, and how do dvh/svh fix it?
en.qsub: When would you use vmin or vmax?
en.what: Definition: vw/vh are viewport‑relative. On mobile, when the address bar hides/shows on scroll, 100vh assumes a fixed (large) viewport and content can be hidden beneath the bar. Fix: dvh (dynamic, changes with the bar), svh (always safe, smaller), lvh (when the bar is removed).
en.why: The 'cut off at the bottom' bug on mobile for full‑screen hero sections or bottom‑fixed buttons occurs because of this. The modern solution is dvh.
cons: Layout can resize on address‑bar scroll when using dvh
gotchas: 100vw includes the vertical scrollbar — horizontal scroll may appear.
dvh can cause jitter during animation/resize; svh is safer.
Write a vh fallback first for older browsers.
terms: Small / large / dynamic viewport height — based on the mobile address bar.
1% of the smaller or larger dimension.

src.name: Reflow vs Repaint vs Composite
src.desc: Layout (reflow) recalculates geometry; paint fills pixels; composite layers GPU-blend. Which props trigger which.
src.q: What is the difference between reflow, repaint, and composite? Which is most expensive?
src.qsub: Give three property changes that force a reflow and three that only repaint.
terms: Elements ki geometry dobara calculate — mehenga.
Pixels dobara bharna (color/shadow badla, geometry nahi).
Layers ko GPU par jodna — sabse sasta.
src.what:
Definition: Property badalne par browser kitna kaam karta hai: layout (width, margin, font-size, top) → paint → composite. Paint-only: color, background, box-shadow. Composite-only: transform, opacity.

Layout badle to paint aur composite bhi hote hain.
src.why: Jitni kam stages trigger hon utna sasta. Isliye animations transform/opacity se karte hain aur DOM ko bar-bar read/write nahi karte.
pros: Pipeline samajhna optimization ka base hai
cons: Properties ki list yaad rakhna padta hai (csstriggers jaisi references)
gotchas: Ek chhota layout change poore subtree ko affect kar sakta hai
display:none se layout hat jata hai, visibility:hidden se nahi
JS mein layout properties padhna (offsetHeight) forced reflow trigger karta hai

en.name: Reflow vs Repaint vs Composite
en.desc: Layout (reflow) recalculates geometry; paint fills pixels; composite layers GPU-blend. Which props trigger which.
en.q: What is the difference between reflow, repaint, and composite? Which is most expensive?
en.qsub: Give three property changes that force a reflow and three that only repaint.
en.what:
Definition: When a property changes, the browser does work: layout (width, margin, font-size, top) → paint → composite. Paint-only: color, background, box-shadow. Composite-only: transform, opacity.

If layout changes, paint and composite also occur.
en.why: The fewer stages triggered, the cheaper. Therefore animations use transform/opacity and avoid repeated DOM read/write.
pros: Understanding the pipeline is the foundation for optimization
cons: You need to remember the list of properties (e.g., csstriggers references)
gotchas: A small layout change can affect an entire subtree
display:none removes layout, visibility:hidden does not
Reading layout properties in JS (e.g., offsetHeight) forces a reflow
terms: Combines layers on the GPU — cheapest.

src.name: Layout Thrashing & Batching
src.desc: Forced synchronous layout from read-after-write in JS; batching reads then writes; requestAnimationFrame.
src.q: What is layout thrashing? How do you avoid forced synchronous layout in a loop?
src.qsub: Which DOM reads force a synchronous layout flush?
terms: Style badalne ke turant baad layout property padhna — browser ko layout turant karna padta hai.
Pehle saare reads, phir saare writes.
Visual updates ko next frame se pehle schedule karna.
src.what: Definition: Layout thrashing tab hoti hai jab loop mein read (offsetHeight) aur write (style.height = ...) alternate hote hain — har read par browser layout recompute karta hai.
src.why: 100 elements ke loop mein 100 layouts ho jate hain; reads batch karne par sirf 1. Ye 'JS se animation/measuring jank karti hai' ka sabse aam kaaran hai.
pros: Bade speedup chhote code change se
cons: Code structure thoda rigid ho jata hai
gotchas: getBoundingClientRect, scrollTop, offsetHeight sab forced layout trigger kar sakte hain
ResizeObserver/IntersectionObserver polling se behtar hain
Frameworks mein bhi effect ke andar read/write mix mat karo

en.name: Layout Thrashing & Batching
en.desc: Forced synchronous layout from read-after-write in JS; batching reads then writes; requestAnimationFrame.
en.q: What is layout thrashing? How do you avoid forced synchronous layout in a loop?
en.qsub: Which DOM reads force a synchronous layout flush?
en.what: Definition: Layout thrashing occurs when a loop alternates reads (offsetHeight) and writes (style.height = ...) — each read forces the browser to recompute layout.
en.why: In a loop over 100 elements, 100 layouts occur; batching reads reduces it to 1. This is the most common cause of 'JS causing animation/measuring jank'.
pros: Large speedup from a small code change
cons: Code structure becomes slightly rigid
gotchas: getBoundingClientRect, scrollTop, offsetHeight can all trigger forced layout
ResizeObserver/IntersectionObserver polling is better
Avoid mixing reads and writes inside effects even in frameworks
terms: Reading a layout property immediately after changing style forces the browser to perform layout immediately.
Do all reads first, then all writes.
Schedule visual updates before the next frame.

src.name: Core Web Vitals (LCP / CLS / INP)
src.desc: Largest Contentful Paint, Cumulative Layout Shift, Interaction to Next Paint; targets and common fixes.
src.q: What are the Core Web Vitals and what causes a poor score in each?
src.qsub: How would you diagnose and fix a high CLS on a page?
terms: Largest Contentful Paint — sabse bada content kab dikha (target ≤ 2.5s).
Cumulative Layout Shift — layout kitna hila (target ≤ 0.1).
Interaction to Next Paint — click/tap ke baad screen kitni jaldi update hui (target ≤ 200ms).
src.what:
Definition: Core Web Vitals real-user experience ke 3 metrics hain: LCP (loading), CLS (visual stability), INP (responsiveness; FID ki jagah aaya).

Fixes: LCP image preload/optimize, CLS ke liye image width/height aur font fallback, INP ke liye long tasks todna.
src.why: Ye Google search ranking signal bhi hain aur directly conversion se jude hain. Lab data (Lighthouse) aur field data (CrUX) alag ho sakte hain; asli users ka data field wala hai.
src.code: /* CLS: jagah reserve */ .ad-slot { min-height: 250px; } img { height: auto; } /* width/height attrs se ratio mil jata hai */ // INP: long task todo await scheduler.yield?.();
where: LCP image aur CLS jaha conversions sensitive hain.
cons: Field data collect karna (RUM) alag effort hai
gotchas: LCP image par lazy-loading mat lagao
Late-loading ads/banners/fonts CLS badhate hain
Lab score acha ho par field INP kharab ho sakta hai

en.name: Core Web Vitals (LCP / CLS / INP)
en.desc: Largest Contentful Paint, Cumulative Layout Shift, Interaction to Next Paint; targets and common fixes.
en.q: What are the Core Web Vitals and what causes a poor score in each?
en.qsub: How would you diagnose and fix a high CLS on a page?
en.what:
Definition: Core Web Vitals are three real-user experience metrics: LCP (loading), CLS (visual stability), INP (responsiveness; replaces FID).

Fixes: preload/optimize LCP images, provide width/height and font fallback for CLS, break up long tasks for INP.
en.why: They are also Google search ranking signals and directly tied to conversion. Lab data (Lighthouse) and field data (CrUX) can differ; field data reflects real users.
cons: Collecting field data (RUM) requires separate effort
gotchas: Do not lazy-load the LCP image
Late-loading ads/banners/fonts increase CLS
Lab score can be good while field INP is poor
terms: Largest Contentful Paint — when the largest content is shown (target ≤ 2.5 s).
Cumulative Layout Shift — how much the layout moves (target ≤ 0.1).
Interaction to Next Paint — how quickly the screen updates after a click/tap (target ≤ 200 ms).
where: LCP image and CLS where conversions are sensitive.

src.name: Recursive CTEs — tree/graph traversal
src.desc: Recursive CTEs call themselves — perfect for hierarchical data like org charts. Has an anchor member (starting row) and recursive step (joins back to CTE). Runs until no new rows are produced.
src.q: How does a recursive CTE work? What are the anchor and recursive members?
src.qsub: How would you find all ancestors in a tree? What prevents infinite loops in recursive CTEs?
terms: WITH RECURSIVE — CTE apne aap ko call kare.
CTE se join karke agli layer — tree/chart nikalna.
Jab koi naya row na bane, loop rukta.
src.what:
Recursive CTE (WITH RECURSIVE) wahi query hai jo apne aap ko refer karti hai — hierarchical data (org chart, category tree, graph) ke liye perfect. Do members:

1) Anchor — shuru ke rows (jaise top manager). 2) Recursive member — anchor ke results ko CTE se join karke agli level. Itna chalta hai jab tak naya row na bane (termination). Har round par duplicate na ho to loop infinite? Careful: PTs cycle ghisha sakte — visited/level column rakho.
src.analogy: Paarivar ki family-tree search: start dada (anchor). "Jis-ka manager ye hai" = recursive step — har person ke manager milte jaate ho. Line khatam (koi manager nahi) to ruk gaye. Cycle (X ka manager Y, Y ka X) — loop hona bad: ek "seen list" rakho.
src.why: Interview me tree/graph problem (all manager chain) — recursive CTE hi ek-line SQL solution. Ye ware un-graph anki expected samajh aati hai — "find all ancestors" repeated question.
src.code:
WITH RECURSIVE org_tree AS (
  -- anchor: top boss
  SELECT id, name, manager_id, 0 AS level
  FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  -- recursive: join back to CTE
  SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, t.level + 1
  FROM employees e
  JOIN org_tree t ON e.manager_id = t.id
)
SELECT * FROM org_tree;

-- RPANIK: cycle = infinite; guard with level/path.
cons: Cycles = infinite loop.

src.name: Big O Notation
src.desc: A language for describing how time and memory grow as input size n grows — ignoring constants and lower-order terms. The first thing an interviewer asks after you propose an algorithm.
src.q: Is O(2n) the same as O(n)?
src.qsub: Why do we ignore constants and lower-order terms? · How do you measure space complexity including recursion stack? · When is O(n log n) actually slower than O(n²) in practice?
src.what:
Do function, bilkul same kaam. 10 items pe dono turant jawab dete hain. 10 lakh items pe ek turant jawab deta hai aur doosra 4 minute le leta hai. Farak code ki khoobsurti mein nahi hai — farak growth mein hai.

Big O usi growth ko likhne ka tarika hai: input n badhega, to kaam kitni tezi se badhega? Ye tumhe seconds nahi batata — ye shape batata hai.

Isiliye stopwatch bekaar hai. Tumhara laptop tez hai, interviewer ka slow, server ka alag. Par O(n²) har machine pe O(n²) hi rehta hai.
src.analogy: Shaadi mein 100 mehmaan. Tum sabse ek-ek baar haath milao — 100 handshakes, O(n). Ab har mehmaan har doosre se mile — 4,950 handshakes. Mehmaan sirf double karo (200), handshakes 4 guna ho jaate hain. Yahi O(n²) ka dard hai.
src.why:
Interviewer "iski complexity kya hai?" isliye puchta hai kyunki ye ek sawaal bata deta hai ki tumne code likha hai ya socha hai. Jo bandaa apne hi solution ki cost nahi bata sakta, wo use improve bhi nahi kar sakta.

Aur asli kaam mein: wo O(n²) loop staging pe 200ms leta hai (100 rows), prod pe 30 second (50,000 rows). Code same, data alag — aur pata tabhi chalta hai jab customer chillata hai.

Kaise sochein:

1. n pehchano — input ka wo hissa jo bada ho sakta hai: array ki length, string ka size, tree ke nodes.
2. Loops aur recursive calls gino. Loop ke andar loop = guna (n × n). Ek ke baad ek loop = jod (n + n).
3. Jod mein sirf sabse bada term rakho — n² + n + 50 ban jata hai n². Kyunki n = 10,000 pe n² = 10 crore hai aur n sirf 10 hazaar — chhota term dikhta hi nahi.
4. Constants phenk do — 3n → O(n).
5. Space alag se gino: extra arrays + recursion ki depth. Ye step 90% log bhool jaate hain.
where: Array index, hash lookup · space: constant
Binary search on sorted input · space: constant
Single linear pass · space: usually constant
Merge/Quick sort, heap ops · space: O(n) for merge

qa.q: Is O(2n) the same as O(n)?
qa.a: Yes — we drop constant factors. Both describe linear growth; the constant doesn't change how the curve scales, and for large n the gap between 2n and n is negligible compared to the gap between n and n².

qa.q: What is the complexity of a while loop that halves n each iteration?
qa.a: O(log n) — each step removes half the input, so it takes log2(n) steps to reach 1. Binary search is the canonical example.

en.name: Big O Notation
en.desc: A language for describing how time and memory grow as input size n grows — ignoring constants and lower-order terms. The first thing an interviewer asks after you propose an algorithm.
en.q: Is O(2n) the same as O(n)?
en.qsub: Why do we ignore constants and lower-order terms? · How do you measure space complexity including recursion stack? · When is O(n log n) actually slower than O(n²) in practice?
en.what:
Both functions do exactly the same work. For 10 items, both respond instantly. For 1,000,000 items, one gives an instant answer while the other takes 4 minutes. The difference is not in code elegance — it is in growth.

Big O is the way to describe that growth: if input n increases, how quickly does the work increase? It doesn't tell you seconds — it tells you the shape.

Therefore a stopwatch is useless. Your laptop may be fast, the interviewer's may be slow, the server may be different. But O(n²) remains O(n²) on every machine.
en.analogy: At a wedding with 100 guests. You shake each guest's hand once — 100 handshakes, O(n). Now every guest meets every other guest — 4,950 handshakes. If you double the guests (200), handshakes become four times larger. That's the pain of O(n²).
en.why:
Interviewer "What is its complexity?" asks because this question shows whether you have written code or just thought about it. Anyone who cannot state the cost of their own solution cannot improve it.

And in real work: that O(n²) loop takes 200 ms in staging (100 rows), 30 seconds in production (50,000 rows). Code is the same, data differs — and you only notice when the customer complains.

How to think:

1. Identify n — the part of the input that can grow: array length, string size, tree nodes.
2. Count loops and recursive calls. Loop inside loop = multiplication (n × n). Loop after loop = addition (n + n).
3. In addition keep only the largest term — n² + n + 50 becomes n². Because when n = 10,000, n² = 100,000,000 and n is only 10,000 — the smaller term is invisible.
4. Discard constants — 3n → O(n).
5. Count space separately: extra arrays + recursion depth. This step is forgotten by 90% of people.

src.name: DFS (Preorder / Inorder / Postorder)
src.desc: Depth-first search visits a node and recurses down one whole subtree before the other. The three orders differ only in WHEN you process the node: before children (pre), between (in), after (post).
src.q: When do you use postorder?
src.qsub: How do you write DFS iteratively? · What's the difference between a 'path' and a 'subtree' in DFS? · Why does preorder + inorder uniquely reconstruct a binary tree?
src.what:
DFS ka matlab: ek subtree mein poora neeche tak jao, tabhi doosre pe aao. Ye ek hi raasta hai — teen "orders" alag traversal nahi hain.

Farak sirf ek baat ka hai: node ko chhuo kab? Bachchon mein jaane se pehle (preorder), left ke baad par right se pehle (inorder), ya dono ke baad (postorder).

Aur ye timing bekaar ki detail nahi hai — problem hi tay karti hai. Jawab bachchon pe depend karta hai (height, diameter)? Postorder. BST se sorted output chahiye? Inorder. Tree copy ya serialize karna hai? Preorder.
src.analogy:
Almirah mein dabbe, dabbon ke andar dabbe. Tum ek dabba kholte ho, uske pehle sub-dabbe mein poori tarah ghus jaate ho, tabhi wapas aa kar doosra kholte ho.
Note kab likhte ho — dabba kholte hi, beech mein, ya band karte waqt — yahi teen orders hain. Raasta wahi ka wahi.
src.why:
Interviewer ye nahi dekhta ki tum teen functions likh sakte ho. Wo dekhta hai ki tum sahi order chun sakte ho ya nahi.

Sabse zyada kaam ka insight: postorder tab chahiye jab node ka jawab uske bachchon ke jawab se banta ho. Height, diameter, "balanced hai kya", "is subtree ka sum" — sab postorder hain. Aur inorder BST ka "secret weapon" hai — sorted output muft mein.

Kaise sochein:

1. if (!node) return — hamesha pehli line.
2. Preorder: node ko process karo → left mein poora jao → right mein poora jao.
3. Inorder: left mein poora jao → node process karo → right mein jao.
4. Postorder: left → right → phir node process karo. Yahan node ke paas dono bachchon ke jawab already hain.
5. Raasta yaad rakhna hai (path problems)? Ek array neeche le kar jao, aur wapas aate waqt pop() kar do — yahi backtracking hai.
6. Time hamesha O(n) — har node ek baar. Space O(h) — stack.

qa.a: When the answer at a node depends on its children's answers — height, diameter, max path sum, balance checks. You must compute children first, which is exactly postorder. Preorder is for when you can decide at the node before descending.

qa.q: What is inorder traversal of a BST useful for?
qa.a: It visits nodes in sorted order. That powers Kth Smallest in a BST and validating a BST (check the sequence is strictly increasing).

en.name: DFS (Preorder / Inorder / Postorder)
en.desc: Depth-first search visits a node and recurses down one whole subtree before the other. The three orders differ only in WHEN you process the node: before children (pre), between (in), after (post).
en.q: When do you use postorder?
en.qsub: How do you write DFS iteratively? · What's the difference between a 'path' and a 'subtree' in DFS? · Why does preorder + inorder uniquely reconstruct a binary tree?
en.what:
DFS means: go all the way down in one subtree before moving to the other. It's a single path — the three \"orders\" are not different traversals.

The only difference is: when do you touch the node? Before visiting children (preorder), after left but before right (inorder), or after both (postorder).

And this timing is not a useless detail — the problem determines it. Does the answer depend on the children (height, diameter)? Postorder. Need sorted output from a BST? Inorder. Want to copy or serialize a tree? Preorder.
en.analogy:
In a cupboard there are boxes, and boxes inside boxes. You open one box, first go completely into its sub‑boxes, then come back and open the next one.
When do you write the note — as soon as you open the box, in the middle, or when you close it — these are the three orders. The path remains the same.
en.why:
The interviewer isn’t looking for whether you can write three functions. They want to see if you can choose the correct order or not.

The most useful insight: you need postorder when a node’s answer is built from its children’s answers. Height, diameter, "is it balanced", "sum of this subtree" — all are postorder. And inorder is the BST’s "secret weapon" — sorted output for free.

How to think:

1. if (!node) return — always the first line.
2. Preorder: process the node → go fully into left → go fully into right.
3. Inorder: go fully into left → process node → go into right.
4. Postorder: left → right → then process node. At this point the node already has both children’s answers.
5. Need to remember the path (path problems)? Carry an array down, and on the way back pop() — that’s backtracking.
6. Time is always O(n) — each node once. Space O(h) — stack.

qa.a: When the answer at a node depends on its children's answers — height, diameter, max path sum, balance checks. You must compute children first, which is exactly postorder. Preorder is for when you can decide at the node before descending.

qa.q: What is inorder traversal of a BST useful for?
qa.a: It visits nodes in sorted order. That powers Kth Smallest in a BST and validating a BST (check the sequence is strictly increasing).

Ek sabzi wala socho. Roz subah wo do haalaton mein se kisi ek mein hota hai — maal khareeda hua paas hai, ya jeb mein sirf paisa hai.
Dono haalaton mein uske aage ke options bilkul alag hain: maal hai to bech sakta hai, paisa hai to khareed sakta hai.
Isliye uska hisaab-kitab ek number nahi, do numbers rakhta hai — "aaj tak ka best, agar maal paas hai" aur "aaj tak ka best, agar nahi hai".
src.why:
Poora Buy and Sell Stock parivaar (I, II, III, IV, cooldown, fee) — chhe alag-alag LeetCode problems — ek hi saanche se ban jaate hain. Sirf states ki ginti badalti hai, soch wahi rehti hai.

Aur isse zyada important: ye sikhata hai ki state kaise badhaayi jaati hai. Jab tumhara DP kaam na kare, aksar wajah yahi hoti hai ki koi zaroori baat state mein daali hi nahi gayi. Ye topic wahi reflex banata hai.

Interview mein ye bahut aam follow-up chain hai: pehle simple version, phir “ab cooldown add karo”, phir “ab at most k transactions”. State machine wale ke liye teeno ek hi cheez hain.

Kaise sochein:

1. States likho — kaunsi baat aage ke options badalti hai? Stock hai / nahi. Cooldown ho to teesra: aaj becha hai.
2. Har state ke transitions likho — is state se kahan-kahan ja sakte ho, aur uski keemat kya hai.
3. Seed karo: cash = 0 (kuch nahi kiya), hold = -Infinity (bina kharide hold karna namumkin hai). Yahan 0 likhna sabse aam bug hai.
4. Har din dono states update karo. Dono lines ko purani values chahiye — isliye cash pehle update karo, ya pehle copy le lo.
5. Aakhir mein jawab cash hai — hold nahi. Haath mein stock rakh ke profit nahi ginta.
6. Fee? Bechte waqt ghata do. Cooldown? Teesra state. k transactions? k ki dimension jodo.

qa.q: What does 'state' mean in state-machine DP?
qa.a: The condition that changes your options — holding vs not holding a share. dp[holding] and dp[cash] evolve day by day: each can 'stay' or 'transition'. Any flag that gates decisions (cooldown, transaction limit) is another state dimension.

qa.q: How does the k-transaction version change?
qa.a: Add k as a dimension: dp[k][holding] vs dp[k][cash]. Buying moves you to the next transaction count. The same transition logic applies, just indexed by how many trades you've used.

en.name: State Machine DP
en.desc: Track multiple STATES of ownership/position per day — for Buy/Sell Stock, whether you currently hold a share. dp[i][state] where state ∈ {not holding, holding}. Transitions model buy/sell/hold decisions.
en.q: What does 'state' mean in state-machine DP?
en.qsub: What does the cooldown state add? · Why start hold at -Infinity? · When is the single-pass min-so-far solution enough?
en.what:
The daily price of a stock is given. Buy, sell, or do nothing — what is the maximum profit?

If you only write dp[i] = “max profit up to day i” you'll get stuck. Because the next decision depends on something that isn't captured in that number: whether you currently hold a stock or not.

If you have the stock, you can sell today. If you don't, you can buy. The options are different.

Therefore, put that information into the state. dp[i][0] = best profit when you do not have the stock, dp[i][1] = best profit when you do have the stock. Now each day each state has only two choices — stay as is, or switch to the other state (by buying or selling).

This is the pattern. It also scales — add a third state for cooldown, add another dimension for k transactions.
en.analogy:
Imagine a vegetable vendor. Every morning he is in one of two situations — the produce is in stock, or only money is in his pocket.
In each situation his future options are completely different: if he has produce he can sell, if he has money he can buy.
Therefore his accounting isn't a single number but two numbers — “best up to today if the produce is in stock” and “best up to today if it isn't”.
en.why:
The entire Buy and Sell Stock family (I, II, III, IV, cooldown, fee) — six different LeetCode problems — can be built from the same template. Only the number of states changes, the thinking stays the same.

And even more important: it teaches how to expand the state. When your DP doesn’t work, the usual reason is that a necessary piece wasn't added to the state. This topic becomes that reflex.

In interviews this is a very common follow‑up chain: first the simple version, then “add cooldown”, then “add at most k transactions”. For the state‑machine approach all three are the same idea.

How to think:

1. Write the states — what factor changes the future options? Whether you have the stock or not. If there is a cooldown, add a third: sold today.
2. Write the transitions for each state — where you can go from this state and what the cost is.
3. Initialize: cash = 0 (nothing done), hold = -Infinity (holding without buying is impossible). Setting it to 0 here is the most common bug.
4. Each day update both states. Both lines need the old values — therefore update cash first, or copy first.
5. At the end the answer is cash — not hold. You don’t count profit while holding stock.
6. Fee? Subtract it when selling. Cooldown? Add a third state. k transactions? Add a dimension for k.

qa.a: Add k as a dimension: dp[k][holding] vs dp[k][cash]. Buying moves you to the next transaction count. The same transition logic applies, just indexed by how many trades you've used.

src.name: Greedy
src.desc: Make the locally optimal choice at each step, hoping it yields the global optimum. Greedy only works when a proof (or strong intuition) shows local choices can't block a better global outcome. Interval scheduling and jump-game are the classics.
src.q: How do you know a greedy is correct?
src.qsub: Why does sorting by end maximize non-overlapping intervals? · When does the two-pointer greedy fail? · How would you disprove a greedy with a counterexample?
src.what:
Greedy ka matlab hai: har step pe wo choice lo jo abhi sabse acchi lag rahi hai, aur peeche mud ke mat dekho. Koi table nahi, koi recursion nahi — ek pass mein kaam khatam.

Jab ye chalta hai to sabse saaf aur sabse tez solution hota hai. Problem sirf ek hai: ye aksar chalta nahi hai, aur jab nahi chalta to koi error nahi aata — bas jawab galat aata hai.

Isliye greedy ka asli kaam code likhna nahi, ye tay karna hai ki greedy chalega ya nahi.

Do tareeke hain. Exchange argument: maano optimal answer ne pehle step pe kuch aur kiya — ab usko greedy wali choice se badal do. Agar answer kabhi kharab nahi hota, to greedy sahi hai. Ya counterexample: ek chhota sa input dhoondo jahan greedy fail ho jaaye. Mil gaya? To greedy nahi chalega — DP nikaalo.
src.analogy:
Ek hi hall mein poore din ki meetings fit karni hain — zyada se zyada meetings.
Instinct kehta hai jo pehle shuru ho use pehle lo. Galat — ek subah 9 baje shuru hoke shaam 6 baje khatam hone wali meeting poora din kha jaayegi.
Sahi rule hai: jo jaldi khatam ho use pehle lo. Hall jitni jaldi khaali hoga, utni zyada meetings ghusengi.
src.why:
Interviewer greedy isliye deta hai kyunki ye sabse aam galti hai. Log DP wali problem pe greedy laga dete hain, 5 test case pass ho jaate hain, aur chhathe pe fail. Wo dekhna chahta hai ki tum pehle soch rahe ho ya seedha likh rahe ho.

Aur jab greedy sahi hota hai, to wo O(n log n) ya O(n) deta hai jahan DP O(n²) leta — ye bada farq hai.

Interval problems (Merge Intervals, Non-overlapping Intervals, Meeting Rooms) aur reachability problems (Jump Game, Gas Station) bahut common hain, aur inka intended solution greedy hi hai.

Ek line jo interview mein bahut acchi lagti hai: “Main pehle ye check kar leta hoon ki greedy safe hai ya nahi — agar exchange argument banta hai to greedy, warna DP.”

Kaise sochein:

1. Greedy rule likho — "har step pe main ye chunuga".
2. Test karo: 3-4 chhote inputs pe haath se chalao. Fail ho gaya? Mubarak ho — DP jaana pad gaya, par 20 minute bach gaye.
3. Saabit karo: exchange argument — optimal ki pehli choice ko apni choice se badlo, aur dekho answer kharab hota hai ya nahi.
4. Sort key sabse important hai. Non-overlapping intervals → end se sort. Merge intervals → start se sort. Ye ulta kiya to sab galat.
5. Ek "best-so-far" variable rakho — sabse door pahunch (Jump Game), current end (scheduling), running sum (Gas Station).
6. Ek hi pass mein chalao. Peeche mudna pade to greedy tha hi nahi.
7. Complexity aksar sort ki wajah se O(n log n) ho jaati hai.
where: O(n log n) or O(n) · space: O(n)

qa.q: How do you know a greedy is correct?
qa.a: Write the exchange argument: if the optimal solution does something different from the greedy at this step, swapping in the greedy choice never worsens the result. Interval scheduling's proof — replacing the first picked interval with the earliest-ending one always works — is the model to imitate.

qa.q: Greedy vs DP — how do you decide fast?
qa.a: If the 'locally best' choice always stays optimal regardless of future input → greedy. If later decisions can undo earlier ones, or the future depends on accumulated choices (subsets, paths) → DP. When unsure, a single counterexample settles it; DP is the safe fallback.

en.name: Greedy
en.desc: Make the locally optimal choice at each step, hoping it yields the global optimum. Greedy only works when a proof (or strong intuition) shows local choices can't block a better global outcome. Interval scheduling and jump-game are the classics.
en.q: How do you know a greedy is correct?
en.qsub: Why does sorting by end maximize non-overlapping intervals? · When does the two-pointer greedy fail? · How would you disprove a greedy with a counterexample?
en.what:
Greedy means: at each step, take the choice that looks best right now, and don’t look back. No table, no recursion — it finishes in one pass.

When it works, it gives the cleanest and fastest solution. The only problem is: it often doesn’t work, and when it fails there’s no error — just a wrong answer.

Therefore the real job of greedy isn’t writing code, but deciding whether greedy will work.

There are two ways. Exchange argument: assume the optimal answer did something different at the first step — replace it with the greedy choice. If the answer never gets worse, greedy is correct. Or counterexample: find a small input where greedy fails. Found one? Then greedy won’t work — use DP.
en.analogy:
In a single hall you need to fit meetings for the whole day — as many meetings as possible.
Instinct says take the one that starts first. Wrong — a meeting that starts at 9 am and ends at 6 pm would consume the whole day.
The correct rule is: take the one that finishes earliest. The sooner the hall becomes free, the more meetings can fit.
en.why:
Interviewers give greedy problems because it’s the most common mistake. People apply a greedy approach to a DP problem, get 5 test cases passed, and then fail the hidden ones. They want to see whether you think first or just code straight away.

And when greedy is correct, it gives O(n log n) or O(n) where DP takes O(n²) — that’s a big difference.

Interval problems (Merge Intervals, Non-overlapping Intervals, Meeting Rooms) and reachability problems (Jump Game, Gas Station) are very common, and their intended solution is greedy.

A line that sounds great in an interview: “I first check whether greedy is safe — if an exchange argument works then greedy, otherwise DP.”

How to think:

1. Write the greedy rule — "at each step I will choose this".
2. Test it: run it by hand on 3‑4 small inputs. Failed? Congrats — you have to use DP, but you saved 20 minutes.
3. Prove it: exchange argument — replace the optimal solution’s first choice with yours and see if the answer gets worse.
4. The sort key is the most important. Non-overlapping intervals → sort by end. Merge intervals → sort by start. Doing the opposite breaks everything.
5. Keep a "best‑so‑far" variable — farthest reach (Jump Game), current end (scheduling), running sum (Gas Station).
6. Run it in a single pass. If you need to go back, greedy wasn’t applicable.
7. Complexity often becomes O(n log n) because of sorting.
where: O(n log n) or O(n) · space: O(n)

en.what:
Definition: The DOM for 10,000 rows overwhelms the browser. In virtualization, only ~20 visible rows are rendered in the DOM; the scrollbar height is faked using a spacer.

In a design round, this is the standard answer for a "large list" — but stating it alone isn’t enough; you need to discuss its tradeoffs.
en.why:
Each DOM node has memory and layout cost. 10k rows cause the browser to freeze for 5‑10 seconds. In a virtualized list, only 20 nodes remain, so 10k and 1 M rows run at roughly the same speed.

But in an interview say — virtualization is not free: Ctrl+F doesn’t work, content isn’t visible to SEO, and variable‑height rows require measurement. Therefore, don’t apply it for up to 200 rows.

Scrolling stays smooth even with 1 M rows
cons: Browser find‑in‑page and SEO both stop working
Scroll can jump with variable‑height rows
Accessibility (screen readers don’t see the full list) requires extra work
gotchas: In an interview, mentioning tradeoffs is essential — just saying "we’ll virtualize" sounds junior
If estimateSize is wrong for variable height, the scrollbar jumps — use measureElement
Don’t virtualize up to 200 rows — a plain list works fine

src.name: Loading / Error / Empty States
src.desc: Skeleton screens vs spinners, error boundaries, retry patterns, empty state UX

data hai hi nahi wala UI

src.what:
Definition: Har data-driven UI ke chaar states hote hain, teen nahi:

  2. Error — kya hua + retry button
  3. Empty — do alag: "kabhi data tha hi nahi" vs "filter se kuch nahi mila"
  4. Success — asli content

Design round mein ye char bolna maturity dikhata hai — junior sirf loading aur success sochta hai.
src.why:
Empty state ke do roop hone chahiye kyunki user ki zaroorat alag hai. "Abhi tak koi order nahi" → usse shopping shuru karne ka button chahiye. "Is filter se kuch nahi mila" → usse filter clear karne ka button chahiye. Ek hi "No data" dikhana dono cases mein bekaar hai.

Aur skeleton spinner se behtar hai kyunki wo layout reserve kar leta hai — content aane pe page koodta nahi (CLS = 0).
where: char states bolna maturity ka signal
har widget ke apne char states
pros: Skeleton se CLS zero — page kood-ta nahi
Sahi empty state se user ko agla kadam pata chalta hai
Retry button se transient network error self-heal ho jaata hai
cons: Char states = char UI banana + maintain karna
Skeleton ko content ke saath sync rakhna padta hai
Zyada skeleton se page "busy" lagta hai
gotchas: Do alag empty states banao — "kabhi data nahi tha" aur "filter se nahi mila" bilkul alag hain
Skeleton ki height asli row jaisi rakho warna content aate hi page koodega
Error mein hamesha retry do — bina retry ke error state dead end hai

en.what:
Definition: Every data-driven UI has four states, not three:

  1. Loading — skeleton (not a spinner, if the shape is known)
  2. Error — what happened + retry button
  3. Empty — two separate: "there was never any data" vs "nothing found with the filter"
  4. Success — actual content

Calling out these four in a design round shows maturity — a junior only thinks about loading and success.
en.why:
Empty state should have two forms because the user's need is different. "No orders yet" → it needs a button to start shopping. "Nothing found with this filter" → it needs a button to clear the filter. Showing a single "No data" in both cases is useless.

Also a skeleton is better than a spinner because it reserves layout — the page doesn’t jump when content arrives (CLS = 0).
pros: Skeleton gives CLS zero — page doesn’t jump
Correct empty state tells the user the next step
Retry button lets a transient network error self‑heal
cons: Four states = four UI pieces to build + maintain
Skeleton must be kept in sync with content
Too many skeletons make the page feel "busy"
gotchas: Create two separate empty states — “never had data” and “not found with filter” are completely different
Keep the skeleton’s height the same as a real row, otherwise the page will shift when content appears
Always provide a retry in the error state — without retry the error state is a dead end
terms: grey placeholder matching the shape of the content
UI for when there is no data at all
Cumulative Layout Shift — page jumping when content arrives
where: each widget has its own four states

en.q: Explain the prototype chain. How does property lookup work in JavaScript?
en.qsub: What is the difference between __proto__ and prototype?
en.what:
In JS, every object has a hidden link—to its prototype. When you request obj.foo and it isn’t on the object, JS follows that link. If it’s not found there, it goes up further, until null.

This chain is called the prototype chain. This is JavaScript’s inheritance.
en.analogy: If you don’t find something at home, you ask the neighbor; if they don’t have it, you ask their neighbor. Eventually you reach a place where there’s no one ahead (null)—then you get undefined.
en.why: That’s why every array has map without it being defined on each one. map lives in one place on Array.prototype—thousands of arrays share it. Memory is saved.
pros: Methods are in one place—thousands of objects share them, saving memory.
Behavior can be added at runtime.
cons: Longer chain lookups are slightly slower.
Modifying built‑in prototypes (monkey‑patching) is dangerous.
People coming from class‑based languages find it confusing.
gotchas: __proto__ and prototype are different: __proto__ exists on an object, prototype exists on a function.
for...in also iterates over inherited properties—Object.keys() does not.
Don’t add your own method to Array.prototype—it will appear on every array and can break libraries.
terms: An object that other objects keep as a "if not found here, look here" reference.
The object's link to its prototype.
The property of a function that becomes the prototype of objects created with new.
where: class internally uses this chain—it’s just nicer syntax.
In DevTools, opening [[Prototype]] shows the entire chain.
en.visualCap: The chain runs from inside to outside. map isn’t on the array, it’s on Array.prototype—and thousands of arrays share that single copy.

en.q: What is a mixin in JavaScript? How does it solve the diamond problem of multiple inheritance?
en.what:
In JavaScript a class can have only one parent. But often behavior is needed from two or three places.

Mixin is the workaround: keep behavior in a plain object or function, and mix it into whatever needs it.
en.why: The classic pain of inheritance: ElectricCar, FlyingCar, ElectricFlyingCar... each combination requires its own class. With mixins, creating a combination becomes like attaching, not like building a new class.
pros: Creating combinations is cheap — no need to create a new class.
Small, separate pieces — easier to test.
cons: Names can clash — if two mixins have the same method, one silently overwrites the other.
"Where did this method come from?" becomes hard to trace.
Too many mixins cause the class behavior to become scattered.

src.name: Tabs with Keyboard Navigation

src.q: Is problem ko kaise solve karoge? Tabs with Keyboard Navigation

  • Clicking a tab shows its panel and hides others

src.name: V8 Engine — what compiles and runs your JavaScript
src.desc: V8 is Google's open-source JS engine written in C++. It compiles JS to machine code using JIT (Just-In-Time) compilation. Node.js is literally a C++ program that embeds V8 and adds OS APIs (file system, networking) on top.

src.name: Module caching, circular dependency handling
src.desc: Node caches modules by resolved filename. Circular deps return partially-built exports (module.exports is returned even if incomplete).
src.q: How does Node.js cache modules and handle circular dependencies?
src.qsub: Circular dependency edge cases show up in large codebases — understanding partial exports is critical.
terms: require by resolved path → same object.
A require B, B require A.
Cache = module ek baar run, sab same instance.
src.what:
Node modules ko resolved filename se cache karta hai. Isliye require('./a') do baar → same object (singleton), code ek baar hi chala.

Circular dependency (A→B→A): jab B A ko require karta hai, A abhi incomplete ho sakta — Node partially-built module.exports return karta hai (jo ab tak set hua). Matlab circular mein aapko wo property nahi milegi jo B ke require ke baad A mein add hui.
src.analogy: Do dost kaam share kar rahe (A aur B). B A se "dairy le aa" maangta hai jab A abhi adha kaam kar raha hai — A wahi de deta jo ab tak bana hai (partial). Poora banana ho to call me function (lazy), jo baad mein resolve ho.
src.why: Circular deps bade codebase mein hoti hai — partial exports se silent undefined bug. Isko jaana = common senior interview. Cache ka matlab bhi singleton — state sharing.
cons: Partial = undefined bug.
Cache complicates hot reload.
Circular growth = design smell.
gotchas: Bas Itna Yaad: resolve cache by filename; circular → partial exports.
Use functions (lazy), not raw values, to dodge partial.

src.name: Getter aur setter — padhne do, badalne mat do
src.desc: Data bahar dikhana hai par badalne nahi dena. Aur setter aksar galat jawab hota hai.
terms: Ek method jo data padh kar deta hai, par badalne nahi deta.
Ek method jo data badalta hai — aur badalte waqt niyam check kar sakta hai.
Aisi value jo store nahi hoti, har baar nikaali jaati hai — jaise "kitni spots khali hain".
src.what:
#earnings private kar diya — par ab report banane wale ko wo chahiye. To kya karein?

Getter banao: ek method jo value padh kar de par badalne na de.

TypeScript mein do tarike hain: normal method (getEarnings()) ya get keyword (get earnings()). Dusre wale ko tum property ki tarah padhte ho — lot.earnings — par wo asal mein ek method hai.
src.why:
Ab ek zaroori baat, jo bahut se OOP tutorials galat sikhate hain.

Har private field ke liye getter aur setter bana dena poore point ko khatam kar deta hai.

Agar tumne #earnings private kiya aur phir setEarnings() bhi bana diya, to tumne kuch nahi bachaya — koi bhi lot.setEarnings(-99999) likh sakta hai. Tumne bas ek lamba raasta bana diya wahi galti karne ka.

Sahi sawaal ye hai: "bahar wale ko is data ke saath kya kaam karna hai?" Report banani hai? To sirf getter do. Fee jama karni hai? To collectFee(amount) do — jo andar niyam check karega.

Kaise karna hai:

Ek achha niyam:

• Getter — jab bahar wale ko value dekhni hai. Aksar sahi.
• Setter — jab bahar wale ko value seedha set karni hai. Aksar galat. Uski jagah ek kaam wala method do (collectFee, park) jo apne andar niyam check kare.

Aur ek chhoti par pyaari cheez: kuch values store karni hi nahi chahiye. "Kitni spots khali hain" ko store karoge to wo purani ho sakti hai. Usko har baar nikaal lo. Aise value ko derived value kehte hain, aur wo kabhi galat nahi ho sakti.
gotchas: Har field ke liye getter+setter banana = private ka poora point khatam. Ye sabse aam OOP galti hai.
Array ya object ka getter seedha andar wali cheez de deta hai — aur bahar wala use badal sakta hai. Copy do ([...arr]) ya readonly do.
get earnings() aur #earnings ka naam ek jaisa nahi ho sakta bina # ke. Isliye TypeScript mein log _earnings likhte hain — par # behtar hai.
Getter ke andar bhaari kaam mat karo. Log samajhte hain ki wo ek property hai (sasta), aur usko loop mein 1000 baar padh lete hain.

src.name: Abstraction kya hai — aur encapsulation se kaise alag
src.desc: Ek data chhupata hai, dusra tarika. Dono ek saath chalte hain.
terms: Andar ka jhanjhat chhupa kar bahar sirf zaroori cheez dikhana.
Ek waada — "main ye kaam kar sakta hu", bina ye bataye ki kaise.
src.what:
Sochо tum gaadi chalate ho. Tum steering ghumate ho aur gaadi mud jaati hai. Tumhe ye jaanne ki zarurat nahi ki andar rack-and-pinion hai ya hydraulic.

Steering wheel ek abstraction hai: wo batata hai ki kya ho sakta hai (mudna), aur kaise hota hai wo chhupa deta hai.

Aur sabse achhi baat: agar company steering ka andar ka mechanism badal de, tumhe dobara gaadi chalana nahi seekhna padta. Yahi abstraction ka poora inaam hai.

Definition: Abstraction means exposing what an object can do while hiding how it does it.
src.why:
Farak yaad rakhne ka sabse aasan tarika:

Encapsulation — "meri tijori ko haath mat lagao." (data)
Abstraction — "tumhe ye jaanne ki zarurat nahi ki tijori kis company ki hai aur uska lock kaise kaam karta hai." (tarika)

Dono ek saath chalte hain. Encapsulation abstraction ko mumkin banata hai: agar data private nahi hoga to tumhara "tarika" chhupega hi nahi, kyunki log data seedha chhoo kar apna tarika bana lenge.

Kaise karna hai:

Hamare parking lot mein abhi abstraction ki do jagah zarurat hai:

1. Payment. ParkingLot ko sirf itna pata hona chahiye: "paisa liya jaa sakta hai". Cash, UPI, card — ye uska sar-dard nahi hona chahiye.

2. Vehicle. Har gaadi ka apna size aur apna rate hai. ParkingLot ko poochna chahiye "tera rate kya hai", na ki khud if-else se decide karna.

Dono ke liye alag auzaar chahiye — aur agli do lessons wahi hain.
gotchas: Abstraction ka matlab "sab kuch chhupa do" nahi hai. Zaroorat se zyada chhupaoge to log workaround dhundhenge. Sirf wo chhupao jo badal sakta hai.
Encapsulation aur abstraction ko interview mein alag karke bata pana zaroori hai. Ek line yaad rakho: encapsulation data chhupata hai, abstraction tarika.

src.name: Subclasses ka pahaad — khud gino
src.desc: Do alag baatein mil kar chaar classes maangti hain. Teen baatein — aath.
terms: Jab do-teen cheezein aapas mein mil kar classes ki ginti kai guna bada dein.
Do baatein jo ek doosre se bilkul azaad hon — jaise "electric hona" aur "handicap hona".
src.what:
Tumhare paas Car, Bike, Truck hain. Ab teen nayi baatein aayin:

• Electric hai ya nahi
• Handicap ke liye hai ya nahi
• VIP hai ya nahi

Ye teeno ek doosre se bilkul azaad hain — ek electric gaadi handicap bhi ho sakti hai aur VIP bhi. Aise azaad baaton ko orthogonal kehte hain.

Ab gino: 3 vehicle types × 2 (electric ya nahi) × 2 (handicap ya nahi) × 2 (VIP ya nahi) = 24 classes.
src.why:
Aur ye sirf ginti ka masla nahi hai. Har nayi baat classes ko dugna kar deti hai:

Ek nayi baat jodo (jaise "diesel hai ya nahi") → 48 classes.
Ek aur → 96.

Aur inme se zyadatar classes mein same code copy hoga. ElectricCar aur ElectricTruck dono mein plugIn() ka wahi code likha hoga — kyunki dono ka baap alag hai aur wo code share nahi kar sakte.

Ye inheritance ki sabse badi seema hai: wo sirf ek dimension mein kaam karta hai.

Kaise karna hai:

Iska jad ye hai: ek class ka sirf ek baap hota hai (Chapter 5 wala niyam). To agar tumhe do azaad baatein ek saath chahiye, to hierarchy mein unke liye jagah hi nahi hai — tumhe har combination ke liye ek nayi class banani padegi.

Aur jab tum ye pahaad khud bana kar ginoge, tab tumhe apne aap samajh aayega ki jawab kya hona chahiye: in baaton ko "class" banane ki jagah "cheez" bana do jo gaadi ke andar rakhi ja sake.

Par abhi jawab mat sochо. Aaj sirf pahaad bana kar gino.
gotchas: Ye code sach mein likho, sirf padhо mat. Aath classes likhne ke baad thakan khud bata degi ki kuch galat hai — aur wahi is chapter ka sabak hai.
Ye mat sochо ki "main itni classes nahi banaunga". Ye classes ek-ek karke, mahino mein banti hain, aur har ek us waqt sahi lagti hai.
Asli codebases mein ye pahaad 3 saal mein khud-ba-khud khada ho jaata hai. Koi ek din baith kar 24 classes nahi banata.

src.name: Immutability aur Value Objects — galat ho hi na sake
src.desc: Ek Money class jo negative ho hi nahi sakti. Aur readonly ka dhokha.
terms: Aisa object jo banne ke baad kabhi badalta nahi. Badalna ho to naya banta hai.
Aisi chhoti class jiski pehchaan uski VALUE se hai, uske id se nahi — jaise ₹100 aur ₹100 ek hi hain.
Har cheez ko number/string rakhna, jabki uske apne niyam hain.
Andar ka array/object bahar dete waqt uski copy dena.
src.what:
Abhi tumhari earnings ek number hai. Aur number ke apne koi niyam nahi hain — wo negative ho sakta hai, NaN ho sakta hai, aur usme rupaye aur paise ka koi farak nahi.

Isko primitive obsession kehte hain: har cheez ko number/string rakhna, jabki us cheez ke apne niyam hain.

Iska ilaaj: ek chhoti Money class banao jo galat ho hi na sake.
src.why:
Aur ab dono ideas ko jodo — immutable value object:

• Banne ke baad kabhi badalta nahi (immutable)
• Uski pehchaan uski value se hai, id se nahi (₹100 aur ₹100 ek hi hain)

Iske teen bade faayde hain: (1) galat state ban hi nahi sakti, (2) kisi ko de do to wo use bigaad nahi sakta, (3) test karna trivial hai.

Kaise karna hai:

Ab ek bahut zaroori baat jo bahut log nahi jaante:

readonly spots: Spot[] — ye array ko immutable nahi banata. Wo sirf this.spots = ... rokta hai. this.spots.push(...) abhi bhi chalta hai!

Do asli tarike:

1. ReadonlyArray<Spot> — ab push par bhi error milegi (compile time).
2. Defensive copy — bahar dete waqt [...this.#spots] do, taaki bahar wala jo chahe kare.
gotchas: readonly array push nahi rokta — ye sabse aam TypeScript galatfehmi hai. ReadonlyArray<T> use karo.
Paise ko float mein mat rakho. 0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3 hota hai. Hamesha paise (integer) mein rakho aur dikhate waqt divide karo.
Har cheez ko value object mat bana do. Jab uske apne niyam hon (Money, PlateNumber, Email) tab banao — plain count ke liye number theek hai.
Value object mein setter mat do. Wo poora point khatam kar deta hai. Badalna ho to naya object return karo.

en.name: Immutability and Value Objects — cannot be wrong
en.desc:
Currently your earnings is a number. And a number has no rules of its own — it can be negative, it can be NaN, and it makes no distinction between rupees and pennies.

This is called primitive obsession: keeping everything as a number/string even though that thing has its own rules.

The remedy: create a small Money class that cannot be wrong.
en.what:
Currently your earnings is a number. And a number has no rules of its own — it can be negative, it can be NaN, and it makes no distinction between rupees and pennies.

This is called primitive obsession: keeping everything as a number/string even though that thing has its own rules.

The remedy: create a small Money class that cannot be wrong.
en.why:
And now combine both ideas — immutable value object:

• Never changes after creation (immutable)
• Its identity is its value, not an id (₹100 and ₹100 are the same)

It has three major benefits: (1) an invalid state cannot be created, (2) if you give it to someone else they cannot corrupt it, (3) testing is trivial.

How to do it:

Now a very important point that many people don’t know:

readonly spots: Spot[] — this does not make the array immutable. It only prevents this.spots = .... this.spots.push(...) still works!

Two real approaches:

1. ReadonlyArray<Spot> — now push will also give an error (compile time).
2. Defensive copy — when exposing, return [...this.#spots] so the outside code can do whatever it wants.
gotchas: readonly array push does not stop — this is the most common TypeScript misconception. Use ReadonlyArray<T>.
Don’t store money as a float. 0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3. Always keep money as an integer and divide when displaying.
Don’t turn everything into a value object. Only create one when it has its own rules (Money, PlateNumber, Email) — a plain number is fine for simple counts.
Don’t give a setter in a value object. It defeats the whole point. If you need to change it, return a new object.
terms: An object that never changes after creation. If it needs to change, a new one is created.
A small class whose identity is its VALUE, not its id — e.g., ₹100 and ₹100 are the same.
Keeping everything as a number/string even though that thing has its own rules.
Returning a copy of an internal array/object when exposing it.
en.visualCap: readonly’s trick: it only prevents reassignment, not internal mutation. And the benefit of a value object: an invalid state cannot be created, and testing is a one‑line job.

src.name: Paanchon ek saath — aur unka rishta
src.desc: Ye alag-alag niyam nahi hain. Ek hi cheez ke paanch pehlu hain.
terms: Paanch niyam: SRP, OCP, LSP, ISP, DIP.
S aur I — cheezein sahi jagah baithi hain ya nahi.
O, L aur D — cheezein kitni juri hui hain.
src.what:
Paanchon ko alag-alag ratna bekaar hai. Wo asal mein do groups mein baithte hain — aur dono groups Chapter 9 wali do cheezein hain:

Cohesion ke niyam (cheezein sahi jagah hain?):
S — ek class, ek badalne ki wajah
I — ek interface, ek tarah ka client

Coupling ke niyam (cheezein kitni juri hain?):
O — naya feature bina purana chhoote jud sake
L — bachcha baap ki jagah chal jaaye
D — business tareeke par nirbhar na ho
src.why:
Aur unka aapas mein rishta ye hai:

L toota → O apne aap toot jaata hai (kyunki instanceof likhna padega)
S toota → I aksar toot jaata hai (badi class ka bada interface banta hai)
D toota → test likhna namumkin (asli database chahiye)
I toota → L aksar toot jaata hai (khaali methods waada todti hain)

Isliye ek ko theek karne se aksar doosre apne aap theek ho jaate hain — jaisa tumne dekha: Chapter 8 mein composition lagane se L aur O dono theek ho gaye the.

Kaise karna hai:

Interview ke liye ek line ka jawab har niyam ke liye — aur saath mein apne code se ek example. Wahi tumhe baaki sabse alag karega:

S — "Ek class, ek badalne ki wajah. Maine ParkingLot se pricing aur notification alag kiye, kyunki unhe finance aur marketing badalwaate the."
O — "Naye ke liye khula, purane ke liye band. Maine PaymentMethod interface banaya; naya wallet payment jodne par ParkingLot mein 0 lines badle."
L — "Bachcha baap ki jagah chale. Mera ElectricCar extends Car isko tod raha tha, to maine use composition mein badla."
I — "Chhote interfaces. Meri Bike ko charge() khaali chhodni pad rahi thi, to maine Chargeable alag kiya."
D — "Business tareeke par nirbhar na ho. ParkingLot SpotRepository par nirbhar hai, PostgresSpotRepo par nahi."
gotchas: SOLID ko checklist ki tarah andha mat chalao. Ye niyam hain, kanoon nahi. Har ek ki apni keemat hai (zyada files, zyada interfaces) aur choti scripts mein wo keemat faayde se zyada ho sakti hai.
Interview mein sirf definition mat batao. Har niyam ke saath apne code ka ek example do — "maine ye toota dekha aur aise theek kiya". Wahi asli jawab hai.
Paanchon ko 100% follow karne ki koshish mein code 3 guna bada ho jaata hai. Sochо: is jagah ye niyam kaunsi asli problem se bacha raha hai?

en.name: Five together — and their relationship
en.desc:
The five rules are not separate gems. They actually belong to two groups — and both groups are the two concepts from Chapter 9:

Cohesion principle (are things in the right place?):
S — a class, a reason to change
I — an interface, a type of client

Coupling principle (how tightly things are linked?):
O — a new feature can be added without breaking the old one
L — a child can replace its parent
D — not dependent on business implementation
en.what:
The five rules are not separate gems. They actually belong to two groups — and both groups are the two concepts from Chapter 9:

Cohesion principle (are things in the right place?):
S — a class, a reason to change
I — an interface, a type of client

Coupling principle (how tightly things are linked?):
O — a new feature can be added without breaking the old one
L — a child can replace its parent
D — not dependent on business implementation
en.why:
And their relationships are:

L broken → O breaks automatically (because you have to write instanceof)
S broken → I often breaks (a large class becomes a large interface)
D broken → testing becomes impossible (real database is required)
I broken → L often breaks (empty methods break promises)

Therefore fixing one often fixes the others automatically — as you saw: applying composition in Chapter 8 fixed both L and O.

How to do it:

For an interview, give a one‑line answer for each principle — and include an example from your code. That will set you apart:

S — "One class, one reason to change. I separated pricing and notification from ParkingLot because finance and marketing needed to change them."
O — "Open for new, closed for old. I created a PaymentMethod interface; adding a new wallet payment changed 0 lines in ParkingLot."
L — "Child replaces parent. My ElectricCar extends Car was breaking it, so I switched to composition."
I — "Small interfaces. My Bike had to leave charge() empty, so I extracted Chargeable."
D — "Not dependent on business implementation. ParkingLot depends on SpotRepository, not on PostgresSpotRepo."
gotchas: Don't treat SOLID as a blind checklist. These are guidelines, not laws. Each has its own cost (more files, more interfaces) and in small scripts that cost can outweigh the benefits.
In an interview, don't just give the definition. Provide a code example for each principle — "I saw this break and fixed it this way". That's the real answer.
Trying to follow the five principles 100% can make the code three times larger. Think: which real problem is this principle actually protecting you from here?
terms: Five principles: SRP, OCP, LSP, ISP, DIP.
S and I — whether things are in the right place.
O, L and D — how tightly things are coupled.

src.name: FCFS, SJF, SRTF
src.desc: First-Come-First-Served: simple, convoy effect. Shortest Job First: optimal avg wait, needs future knowledge.
src.q: Compare FCFS and SJF. What is the convoy effect? Why is SJF optimal but impractical?
src.qsub: What is starvation? How does aging solve it?
terms: First Come First Served — jo pehle aaya wo pehle (queue jaisa).
Ek lamba process sab ko piche rokh deta hai — traffic jam.
Shortest Job First — sabse chhota kaam pehle. Optimal avg wait.
Shortest Remaining Time First — preemptive SJF.
Chote processes aate rahein to lamba kabhi nahi chattas — bhuka reh jaata.
Purane processes ki priority badhao taaki bhuke na rahein.
src.what:
FCFS — sabse simple. Jo process pehle bazaar aayi usi ko CPU. Order = arrival order. Dikkt: ek lamba process aaye to uske piche saare lambe intezaar mein — convoy effect (traffic jam).

SJF — sabse chhota kaam pehle. Yeh average wait time ko optimal banata hai. Par problem: future nahi pata (kaun sa kitna lama hai), aur chhote aate rahein to bada starvation se bhukha mar jaata.

SRTF — SJF ka preemptive version: jab bhi naya chhota aata hai, chalti process ko rok kar use de do.
src.analogy:
Billing/ATM ki line:
• FCFS — jo pehle khada wo pehle. Agar saamne waale ka kaam 10 minute ka hai aur tumhare aage sab ka 1 minute, to tum 10 minute intezaar karoge (convoy).
• SJF — sabse pehle wo serve karo jiska kaam sabse chhota. Line tez khatam (optimal), par agar chhoote aate rahein to bade wale kabhi turn nahi paenga (starvation).
src.why: FCFS realistic to hai par wasteful (convoy). SJF average ke liye best hai par future prediction aur starvation ki problem. In dono se concepts clear hote hain — preemption, optimality, starvation, aging — jo baaki algorithms mein bhi use hote.
pros: FCFS simple, koi starvation nahi (fair order).
cons: FCFS convoy effect — lamba traffic jam.
SJF future ka duration pata nahi.
SJF starvation — bada process bhuka.
gotchas: Bas Itna Yaad: FCFS = jo pehle, SJF = jo chhota. Convoy = ek lamba sab roke. Starvation = chhote aaye to bada bhuka.
SJF optimal isliye kyunki chhote pehle karne se bade ka wait "comparatively" kam hota.
SRTF (preemptive SJF) response better deta hai par aur zyada overhead.

en.q: Compare FCFS and SJF. What is the convoy effect? Why is SJF optimal but impractical?
en.what:
FCFS — the simplest. The process that arrives first gets the CPU. Order = arrival order. Problem: if a long process arrives, all others wait behind it — convoy effect (traffic jam).

SJF — the smallest job first. This makes the average waiting time optimal. But the problem: the future is unknown (which job is how long), and if short jobs keep arriving, the long one starves.

SRTF — preemptive SJF: whenever a new shorter job arrives, the running process is preempted and given to it.
en.analogy:
Billing/ATM line:
• FCFS — first in line, first served. If the person ahead has a 10‑minute task and everyone behind has 1‑minute tasks, you will wait 10 minutes (convoy).
• SJF — serve the smallest task first. The line clears quickly (optimal), but if short tasks keep arriving, the long one may never get a turn (starvation).
en.why: FCFS is realistic but wasteful (convoy). SJF is best for average waiting time but has the problem of future prediction and starvation. Both clarify concepts — preemption, optimality, starvation, aging — which are also used in other algorithms.
pros: FCFS is simple, no starvation (fair order).
Helps understand concepts like preemption, starvation, aging.
cons: FCFS convoy effect — long traffic jam.
SJF does not know future durations.
SJF starvation — long process starves.
gotchas: Just remember: FCFS = first, SJF = shortest. Convoy = a long job blocks everyone. Starvation = when short jobs arrive, the long one starves.
SJF is optimal because processing short jobs first reduces the wait of longer jobs "comparatively".
SRTF (preemptive SJF) gives better response but adds more overhead.
terms: First Come First Served — the one that arrived first goes first (like a queue).
A long process blocks everyone behind it — traffic jam.
Shortest Job First — the smallest job first. Optimal average wait.
Shortest Remaining Time First — preemptive SJF.
If short processes keep arriving, the long one never gets CPU — it starves.
Increase the priority of older processes so they don’t starve.
