en.visualCap: FCFS: convoy effect makes the line long. SJF: shortest first, line clears quickly.

src.name: Message Queues & Sockets
src.desc: Message queues: asynchronous, typed messages. Sockets: network or Unix domain, bidirectional, flexible.
src.q: Compare message queues, shared memory, and sockets for IPC. When would you choose each?
src.qsub: What is a Unix domain socket? How does it differ from a TCP socket in performance?
terms: Typed messages ka queue — processes ek-doosre ki taraf push/recv.
Bhejne wala wait nahi karta — message queue mein jaata.
Har message ka ek type/label — selective receive.
Same machine — TCP jaisa interface, par kernel-local, fast.
src.what:
Message queue — processes structed messages bhejti hain (type + data). Bhejne wala wait nahi karta (async), OS queue mein rakhta. Alag tarike se: sockets — bidirectional byte connection, local (Unix domain) ya network (TCP).

Message queues decouple — producer/consumer alag speed; queue buffer. Sockets flexible — serve-request pattern, network bhi. Shared memory se slow par safe/simple.
src.analogy: Office mail system: tum box (message queue) mein note daalte ho, receiver baad mein aakar uthta hai — tum ruke nahi (async). Har note par type (e.g. "urgent") hota hai. Sockets = direct telephone line — do-way, turant, dono baat karte. Message queue = post office (async), socket = phone call (sync).
src.why: Jab processes ko data structure wise baat karni ho aur daau hi daalu na chahiye — message queue ideal. Jab request-response ya network ho — sockets. Ye IPC choices ka practical toolkit hai: speed (shared) vs convenience (message) vs flexibility (socket).
cons: Slower than shared memory (copy).
Queue overflow/limits handle karna.
Socket sync setup overhead.
gotchas: Bas Itna Yaad: message queue = async typed queue; socket = bidirectional connection (local/network).
Message queue decouples (producer→queue→consumer).
Interview: "when shared memory vs message vs socket" — speed vs convenience vs network.

en.what:
Message queue — processes send structured messages (type + data). The sender does not wait (async), the OS keeps them in a queue. Alternatively: sockets — bidirectional byte connection, local (Unix domain) or network (TCP).

Message queues decouple — producer and consumer can run at different speeds; queue acts as a buffer. Sockets are flexible — support serve‑request pattern, also work over network. Shared memory is slower but safe/simple.
en.analogy: Office mail system: you put a note in a box (message queue), the receiver later comes and picks it up — you don’t wait (async). Each note has a type (e.g. "urgent"). Sockets = direct telephone line — two‑way, immediate, both talk. Message queue = post office (async), socket = phone call (sync).
en.why: When processes need to communicate data‑structure‑wise and don’t want tight coupling — message queue is ideal. When there is a request‑response or network communication — sockets. This is a practical toolkit for IPC choices: speed (shared memory) vs convenience (message queue) vs flexibility (socket).
gotchas: Just remember: message queue = async typed queue; socket = bidirectional connection (local/network).
Message queue decouples (producer→queue→consumer).
Interview: "when shared memory vs message vs socket" — speed vs convenience vs network.
terms: Typed messages queue — processes push to and receive from each other.
Sender does not wait — goes into the message queue.
Each message has a type/label — selective receive.

src.what:
Definition: useEffect(fn, deps) React ko kehta hai "commit + paint ke baad ye kaam karo". deps array batati hai kab dobara chalana hai.

  • Koi array nahi → har render
  • [] → sirf mount pe (aur StrictMode dev mein 2 baar)

en.name: useEffect — Timing, Deps, Cleanup
en.desc: Runs after paint, asynchronously. The dependency array controls when it re-runs. The cleanup function runs before the next effect or on unmount.
en.q: Explain useEffect's full lifecycle: when does it run, when does cleanup run, what is the dependency array contract?
en.qsub: What happens if you put a function in the dependency array? How do you fix the infinite loop?
en.what:
Definition: useEffect(fn, deps) tells React "after commit + paint do this work". The deps array indicates when to run again.

  • No array → every render
  • [] → only on mount (and twice in StrictMode development)
  • [a, b] → when a or b change

Cleanup runs every time before the effect runs again — not only on unmount.
en.analogy: Turning off the light when leaving a room. You turn it off every time you leave — not just when you move out of the house.
en.why:
Running cleanup every time prevents race conditions. If you switch users quickly, three fetches may start. Without cleanup, the one that finishes last wins, even if it belongs to an old user. Aborting in cleanup ensures only the latest request survives.

React 18 guidance: useEffect is not ideal for data fetching. Use React Query or a framework loader — they handle caching, deduplication, retries.
pros: Setup and cleanup in one place — less chance of forgetting
cons: Wrong tool for data fetching — leads to waterfall and race conditions
Incorrect deps cause infinite loops or stale data
Object/function deps change on every render
gotchas: For things that can be calculated during render, create a memoized value (MAT) with effect + state
Do not use object/function as deps — extract primitives or use useMemo/useCallback
Do not silence the eslint exhaustive-deps warning — understand it, it is often correct
terms: work that runs outside of render — fetch, timer, subscription, DOM
values whose changes cause the effect to re‑run
function returned by the effect — runs before the next effect

en.name: useRef — Beyond DOM Access
en.desc: useRef returns a stable object { current } that persists across renders without triggering re-renders. Use it for: DOM access, timers, previous values, and mutable instance variables.
en.q: What are the three main uses of useRef? How is it different from useState for storing values?

en.what:
Definition: useRef(init) returns an object { current: init } that remains the same object for the entire component lifecycle. Changing .current does not cause a re‑render.

Two uses: (1) capture a DOM node, (2) store a value that persists but does not affect the UI (timer id, previous value, flag).
en.analogy: Pocket. You can put anything in it, take it out — no one needs to be notified (no re‑render). State is a notice board — when something changes, everyone sees it.
en.why: Sometimes you need to remember a value but the UI does not depend on it — interval id, a "is first render" flag, previous props. If you store it in state, every change would cause an unnecessary render. Ref fills exactly this gap.
pros: Changing the value is free — no render
Same object for the whole lifetime — reference stable
cons: Reading/writing ref during render violates React rules
Overusing makes code imperative and untraceable
Changing a ref does not update the UI — forgetting this can cause bugs
gotchas: Changing ref.current will NOT update the UI — use state if you need to display it
Do not read/write ref.current during render — do it after commit (in effect or event)
ref.current is set at commit time — it is null during the first render

en.desc: A component re-renders when: its state changes, its parent re-renders, context it consumes changes, or its key changes. Props being the same is NOT enough to prevent re-renders.
en.q: List every cause of a React re-render. What is the most common source of unnecessary re-renders in production apps?
en.qsub: If a parent re-renders but passes the same props to a child, does the child re-render? What stops it?
en.what:
Definition: A component re-renders for only four reasons:

  1. Its own state changed
  2. Its parent re-rendered
  3. A context value it consumes changed
  4. Its hook (useSyncExternalStore etc.) sent an update

Changing props is not in the list — props change only when the parent renders, so the actual reason is #2.
en.why: The biggest misconception: "render happened because props changed". The truth is the opposite — the child rendered because the parent rendered, even if the props are exactly the same. Understanding this reveals the proper optimization path: preventing the parent’s render or pushing state down is more effective than memoizing props.
pros: Four reasons — the complete list is right here, nothing else
Pushing state down is the cleanest fix
Composition is better and cheaper than memo
cons: Finding the cause in a large tree takes time

src.name: Works locally, broken in production
src.desc: The classic. Likely causes across build, env, network, caching, and data.
src.q: Is problem ko kaise solve karoge? Works locally, broken in production
src.what:
“A feature you built works perfectly in local dev but misbehaves in production. What are the likely causes and how do you debug it?”

Concepts: Prod builds · Env vars at build time · CORS · SameSite cookies · CDN caching · Staging parity

Kya test hota hai: Do you understand dev vs prod differences, not just your framework.
src.why:
• List the categories of difference: build, env vars, network/CORS, caching/CDN, data.
  • First move: run a production build locally — that splits build issues from infra issues.
src.answer:
Likely difference categories

  • Build: minification breaking code, tree-shaking removing something, NODE_ENV=production changing library behavior.
  • Env vars: missing/wrong API_URL or keys — frontend env vars are baked in at build time; the prod build may have been built with different values.
  • Network: CORS (localhost whitelisted, prod domain isn't), HTTPS vs HTTP, cookies with SameSite/Secure behaving differently across domains.
  • Caching/CDN: user getting a stale bundle or a stale API response cached at the CDN.
  • Data: prod data has shapes/nulls/volumes your local seed data never had.

Debug approach

  • Reproduce with a production build locally first — isolates build issues from infra issues.
  • Open prod, check console + network tab: failed requests, 4xx/5xx, CORS errors, wrong URLs.
  • Diff env configs between environments.

Prevent

  • A staging environment that mirrors prod (same build, same infra), e2e tests against staging, config validation at startup.

Staff+ Analysis

  • Systemic issue: "Works locally" bugs are a staging-parity failure. Staff+ engineers invest in staging environments that mirror prod — same build artifacts, same config generation, same data volume profiles. The cost of staging is justified by eliminating entire classes of prod-only bugs.
  • Build pipeline hygiene: Frontend env vars baked at build time is an anti-pattern. Use runtime config (injected via server-side template or a /config endpoint) so the same build deploys to all environments. This eliminates env-mismatch bugs.
  • Data-driven testing: Prod-like data in staging (anonymized subsets of real data with edge cases) catches data-shape bugs before deploy. Automate the data refresh process so staging data is never more than 24 hours stale.
  • Developer workflow: A "prod build locally" command should be one step. Make it easy for every developer to run the exact production build on their machine — this catches most env-difference bugs before they reach staging.

Follow-ups

src.name: Users randomly logged out / intermittent 401s
src.desc: Backend says auth is healthy. Token refresh races, tabs, cookies.
src.q: Is problem ko kaise solve karoge? Users randomly logged out / intermittent 401s
src.what:
“Some users report being logged out mid-session at random. The backend team says the auth service is healthy. Investigate.”

Concepts: Access vs refresh tokens · Refresh race · Token rotation · Multi-tab auth · SameSite / Secure · Interceptors

Kya test hota hai: Full-stack auth understanding — tokens, refresh flows, race conditions.
src.why:
• Correlate timing: 401s exactly N minutes after login = access-token expiry → the refresh flow is failing.
  • Classic bug: two parallel 401s both refresh with a single-use refresh token — second one fails → logout. Single-flight the refresh.
src.answer:
1. Gather evidence

  • When do 401s happen? Roughly N minutes after login = token expiry → refresh flow failing. Truly random = something else.
  • Check network logs for the refresh call: is it firing, failing, or racing?

2. Common root causes

  • Refresh race: two parallel API calls both get 401, both try to refresh with the same refresh token; with rotation (single-use), the second refresh fails and logs the user out. Fix: single-flight the refresh — queue concurrent requests behind one refresh promise.
  • Multiple tabs: each tab refreshing independently invalidates the other's token. Fix: share tokens via one source (cookie or BroadcastChannel coordination).
  • Cookies: SameSite/Secure/domain misconfig so the cookie isn't sent on some requests.
  • Server side: sticky-session loss behind a load balancer if sessions are in-memory per instance.

3. Prevent

  • Centralized API client with a 401→refresh→retry-once interceptor; alerting on refresh-failure rate; e2e test covering token expiry.

Staff+ Analysis

  • Systemic issue: Random logouts are almost always a race-condition bug in the token refresh flow. Staff+ engineers treat token management as a system-wide concern — create a shared auth client that handles refresh single-flight, retry queuing, and multi-tab coordination. Every service should use the same client.
  • Architecture: The refresh race is a symptom of a deeper problem: parallel API clients competing for auth state. The fix is a centralized API client with a request interceptor that handles 401 → refresh → retry as an atomic operation, queuing concurrent requests behind a single refresh promise.
  • Multi-tab strategy: Use BroadcastChannel or service worker to coordinate auth state across tabs. When one tab refreshes the token, all other tabs should receive the new token. This prevents the "log out because another tab refreshed" pattern.
  • Cookie vs localStorage trade-off: httpOnly cookies prevent XSS token theft but require careful CSRF protection and have cross-origin limitations. localStorage is simpler for SPA auth but is XSS-vulnerable. The industry trend is toward httpOnly cookies with BFF (Backend-for-Frontend) pattern.

src.name: Search input fires 300+ requests with no debounce
src.desc: Typing "production debugging" sends a request on every keystroke. 300+ network requests fired.
src.q: Is problem ko kaise solve karoge? Search input fires 300+ requests with no debounce
src.what:
"Users type in a search box and the network tab shows hundreds of requests being fired — one per keystroke. The server is getting hammered. You see 300+ requests for a single search query. Design the fix."

Concepts: Debounce · AbortController · Request cancellation · React Query deduplication · Minimum query length · Search-as-you-type patterns

Kya test hota hai: Debounce/throttle patterns, AbortController, request cancellation, and the search UX best practices.
src.why:
• Debounce delays the request until the user stops typing for N milliseconds. Without it, every keystroke fires immediately.
  • Even with debounce, you still need to cancel in-flight requests when a new one fires — otherwise old responses can arrive after newer ones.
src.answer:
1. Triage

  • Check the Network tab — confirm the requests are firing on every keystroke. Check the response times and whether the server is throttling or returning errors under load.

2. Investigate

  • The search handler calls the API directly on every input change with no delay. For a 20-character query, that is 20 requests (or more if the user backspaces and retypes).
  • Two issues: (1) no debounce (requests fire too often) and (2) no cancellation (old requests still consume server resources and can overwrite newer results when they arrive).

3. Fix

  • Debounce the search input (200-300ms) — use useDeferredValue (React 18+) or a debounce utility (lodash.debounce, custom hook).
  • Add AbortController: cancel the previous in-flight request when a new one fires. In React, do this in the useEffect cleanup or the fetch wrapper.
  • Add a minimum query length (e.g. 3 characters) to avoid searching for single characters.
  • For advanced deduplication, use React Query or SWR which handle caching, deduplication, and stale-while-revalidate automatically.

4. Prevent

  • Create a shared useDebouncedSearch hook that all search inputs use. Add a lint rule that flags fetch calls inside onChange handlers without debounce. Add a server-side rate limit as a backstop.

Staff+ Analysis

  • Systemic issue: This is a missing abstraction problem — the team does not have a standard search hook or component. Staff+ engineers create a useSearch or DebouncedInput component that all search UIs use, with debounce, minimum length, AbortController, and error handling built in.
  • Architecture: The ideal search flow: user types, debounce (200ms), minimum length check, cancel previous request, fire new request, display results. This should be one reusable hook, not copy-pasted per search input.
  • Server-side defense: Even with client-side debounce, add server-side rate limiting on search endpoints. A malicious user or a bot can bypass client-side controls. Rate limiting is the real protection.
  • UX consideration: Show a loading indicator during the debounce delay. Display "no results for short queries" for queries under the minimum length. Consider showing cached results instantly while the new request fires (stale-while-revalidate).

src.name: Polling never stops — 10,000+ requests overnight
src.desc: Tab left open makes 10,000+ polling requests. setInterval never cleared when tab hidden.
src.q: Is problem ko kaise solve karoge? Polling never stops — 10,000+ requests overnight
src.what:
"A user left their browser tab open overnight. In the morning, the network tab shows over 10,000 polling requests were made and their laptop fan is spinning. The app uses setInterval for polling. Investigate and fix."

Concepts: setInterval cleanup · Page Visibility API · document.hidden · Polling budget · WebSocket for real-time · useEffect cleanup

Kya test hota hai: Timer lifecycle management, Page Visibility API, and resource-conscious polling patterns.
src.why:
• setInterval runs even when the tab is in the background — the browser throttles it to once per second but it never stops. Over 8 hours at 1 request/second, that is 28,000 requests.
  • Use the Page Visibility API (document.visibilitychange) to pause polling when the tab is hidden, and clear the interval in the useEffect cleanup on unmount.
src.answer:
1. Triage

  • Check the network tab: confirm the polling requests are firing at a steady rate. Check if the tab was backgrounded — browsers throttle background tabs to ~1 request/second for setInterval but do not stop it.
  • Check server impact: was the polling endpoint designed for this volume? Is it causing database load?

2. Investigate

  • The polling is set up with setInterval(fetchData, 5000) but never cleared. There is no cleanup on component unmount (missing useEffect return) and no visibility change handler.
  • Even if the component unmounts, the interval reference may be held by a closure, preventing garbage collection.

3. Fix

  • Clear the interval on unmount: return () => clearInterval(intervalId) in the useEffect cleanup.
  • Pause polling when the tab is hidden: add a visibilitychange listener that clears the interval when document.hidden is true and restarts it when the tab becomes visible again.
  • Consider replacing polling with WebSocket or Server-Sent Events (SSE) for truly real-time data — this eliminates the polling problem entirely.

4. Prevent

  • Create a usePolling hook that handles cleanup, visibility, and backoff. Add a lint rule that flags setInterval without clearInterval. Monitor polling request volume in RUM to detect runaway polling early.

Staff+ Analysis

  • Systemic issue: Polling without lifecycle management is a resource leak — it wastes bandwidth, server resources, and battery. Staff+ engineers treat polling as a last resort and prefer push-based patterns (WebSocket, SSE, push notifications) for real-time data.
  • Architecture: If polling is necessary (e.g. compatibility constraints), it must be wrapped in a usePolling hook that: (1) clears on unmount, (2) pauses on visibility change, (3) adjusts frequency based on data freshness (poll more often when data changes, less when stale), (4) has a maximum concurrent poll budget per page.
  • Org-level prevention: Add a server-side rate limit on polling endpoints (e.g. max 1 request per 5 seconds per user). Add a lint rule that flags setInterval without corresponding clearInterval. Monitor the polling request volume per endpoint in production.
  • Battery and performance: Background polling drains battery and wastes mobile data. On mobile, the browser may throttle background tabs more aggressively, but the requests still fire. The Page Visibility API is the correct solution — it is well-supported across all modern browsers.

Follow-ups

src.name: Notification System
src.desc: Design a UI notification system that informs without overwhelming.
src.q: Is problem ko kaise solve karoge? Notification System
src.what:
"How would you design a notification system in the UI that does not overwhelm the user?"

Concepts: Toast notifications · Notification queue · Priority levels · Auto-dismiss timers · Notification center · Sound and badge indicators

Kya test hota hai: Toast management, notification stacking, priority levels, and auto-dismiss timing.
src.why:
• Use a notification queue with a maximum visible count (e.g., 3). New notifications stack in the queue and appear as old ones dismiss. This prevents screen flooding.
  • Categorize notifications by priority: errors are persistent until dismissed, warnings auto-dismiss after 10 seconds, and info toasts dismiss after 5 seconds. Different visual styles for each priority.
src.answer:
1. Triage

  • Identify notification sources: user actions (save success), system events (new message), background processes (sync complete), and errors (API failure). Each source may need different handling.
  • Define constraints: max visible notifications (3-5), position on screen (top-right for desktop, top for mobile), and stacking behavior.

2. Investigate

  • The problem with naive toast implementations: every API response triggers a toast, leading to 5+ notifications stacking on screen. Users dismiss them all without reading, defeating the purpose.
  • Good notification design: only notify for non-obvious events. A green flash on a saved button is better than a "Saved!" toast. Reserve toasts for errors, warnings, and background event completions.

3. Fix

  • Build a NotificationManager class: show({ type, message, duration, priority }). Maintains a queue of max 3 visible notifications. New notifications enter the queue; if the queue is full, the oldest non-persistent notification is dismissed to make room.
  • Implement auto-dismiss: info (5s), success (3s), warning (10s), error (manual dismiss only). Pause the auto-dismiss timer on hover so the user can read long messages.
  • Add a notification center (bell icon) that shows a dropdown of recent notifications. This is the safety net — if a notification was dismissed before the user saw it, they can find it in the center. Badge the bell with unread count.

4. Prevent

  • Review notification triggers quarterly. Remove notifications that users consistently dismiss within 1 second (they are noise). A/B test notification copy and timing. Log notification interaction rates to identify which notifications are useful and which are annoying.

Staff+ Analysis

  • Notification philosophy: The best notification is no notification. Every notification is an interruption. Staff engineers work with product to reduce notification volume, not increase it. Reserve notifications for events that require user attention or action.
  • Cross-tab coordination: When the user has multiple tabs open, each tab may independently show notifications for the same event. Use BroadcastChannel or SharedWorker to coordinate — only the active tab shows the notification, others update their badge count silently.
  • Notification debt: Over time, teams add notification triggers without removing old ones. The notification system becomes a source of noise. Establish a policy: every new notification must justify its existence, and old notifications are reviewed quarterly. Track notification dismissal rate as a health metric.
  • Accessibility: Notifications must be announced to screen readers via aria-live="assertive" (errors) or aria-live="polite" (info). Visual-only notifications exclude deaf and blind users. Provide a visual indicator (badge, color change) alongside the toast.

Follow-ups

Kya test hota hai: Tab order, focus indicators, keyboard shortcuts, focus traps in modals, and skip navigation.
src.why:
• Tab through every interactive element on the page. The order should follow the visual layout (top-to-bottom, left-to-right). If it does not, you need to adjust tabindex or reorder the DOM.
  • Every focusable element must have a visible focus indicator. The browser default (blue outline) works. Never use outline: none without providing a custom focus style — this makes the app unusable for keyboard users.
src.answer:
1. Triage

  • Identify all interactive elements: buttons, links, inputs, selects, checkboxes, radios, custom dropdowns, modals, and any element with onClick handlers. Each must be focusable and operable via keyboard.
  • Test the complete user flow with keyboard only: sign in → navigate to feature → interact with controls → complete task. Note every point where you need a mouse.

2. Investigate

  • Common keyboard navigation failures: (1) custom components not in the tab order (missing tabIndex), (2) focus hidden behind a modal (no focus trap), (3) dropdown menus not navigable with arrow keys, (4) focus ring removed with outline: none, (5) skip navigation link missing (user must tab through 50 nav links to reach content).
  • Test with a screen reader to verify that focus announcements match what the user expects. If a custom button does not announce as a button, it needs role="button".

3. Fix

  • Ensure every interactive element is in the natural tab order. Use tabIndex={0} only when semantic HTML cannot represent the element. Never use positive tabIndex values (tabIndex="1") — they break natural tab order.
  • Add a visible focus indicator: :focus-visible is the modern selector that shows focus only for keyboard users (not mouse clicks). Style it with a 2px solid outline with an offset: outline: 2px solid #005fcc; outline-offset: 2px.
  • Implement focus management: skip navigation link at the top of the page, focus trap in modals (Tab cycles within the modal, Escape closes it and returns focus to the trigger), and arrow key navigation in lists, menus, and toolbars.

4. Prevent

  • Add keyboard navigation testing to your CI: Playwright has page.keyboard.press("Tab") for automated tab-through testing. Add a "keyboard audit" step to PR reviews for UI changes. Track the percentage of interactive elements that are keyboard-accessible.

  • Systemic accessibility: Keyboard navigation is not a feature — it is a fundamental requirement. Staff engineers ensure every new component is keyboard-accessible before it ships. This means the component library must include keyboard navigation by default, not as an add-on.
  • Focus management architecture: Design a centralized focus management system that handles: page navigation (focus the main heading), modal open/close (trap and restore), dynamic content (announce to screen readers), and error recovery (focus the first error field). This prevents ad-hoc focus management that breaks in edge cases.
  • Testing automation: Automated keyboard testing catches ~60% of issues: tab order, focus visibility, and basic interaction. The remaining 40% (screen reader announcements, complex interaction patterns, semantic correctness) requires manual testing with assistive technology. Budget time for both.
  • Keyboard shortcuts: For power users, keyboard shortcuts (Ctrl+K for search, Ctrl+/ for help) dramatically improve productivity. But they must not conflict with screen reader shortcuts. Document all shortcuts and provide a shortcut reference panel (Ctrl+/ shows all shortcuts).

src.name: Deploy causes 502s for 10 seconds every time
src.desc: In-flight requests dropped when pods are killed — no graceful drain configured.
src.q: Is problem ko kaise solve karoge? Deploy causes 502s for 10 seconds every time
src.what:
“Every deploy causes a spike of 502 errors lasting about 10 seconds. Users see blank pages or failed API calls. The health checks pass quickly and the new pods are ready. Why are requests being dropped during the transition?”

Concepts: Graceful shutdown · Connection draining · SIGTERM handler · PreStop hooks · Load balancer deregistration · TerminationGracePeriodSeconds

Kya test hota hai: Graceful shutdown, connection draining, and the gap between "pod ready" and "old pod fully drained".
src.why:
• The load balancer still sends traffic to a pod after SIGTERM is received. If the pod kills connections immediately, those in-flight requests become 502s.
  • The Kubernetes preStop hook + sleep gives the load balancer time to deregister the pod before it stops accepting connections.
src.answer:
1. Triage

  • Check deploy logs: how long between SIGTERM and pod termination? If the app exits immediately on SIGTERM, in-flight requests are killed.
  • Check the load balancer target group: is the pod deregistered BEFORE or AFTER the pod stops accepting traffic? If after, requests route to a dead pod.

2. Root cause

  • The app does not handle SIGTERM — it exits immediately, dropping all in-flight connections.
  • Even with a SIGTERM handler, the Kubernetes service has not yet removed the pod from the endpoint list, so the load balancer continues routing to it.
  • The default terminationGracePeriodSeconds (30s) may be too short for long-running requests.

3. Fix

  • Add a SIGTERM handler that stops accepting NEW connections, drains in-flight requests (with a timeout), then exits.
  • Add a preStop hook with a sleep 5 so Kubernetes delays the SIGTERM until the pod is fully deregistered from the service endpoints.
  • Increase terminationGracePeriodSeconds to accommodate your longest request duration.

4. Prevent

  • Add a "connections draining" metric to monitor how many in-flight requests are in progress during shutdown. Test graceful shutdown in staging by sending long-running requests and triggering a rolling restart.

Staff+ Analysis

  • Systemic issue: Graceful shutdown is almost never tested — teams assume the framework handles it, but frameworks typically only close the listener socket, not drain in-flight requests. Staff+ engineers enforce a graceful-shutdown contract: every service must implement drain logic and it must be tested in staging.
  • Architecture: The full shutdown sequence: (1) preStop hook sleeps to deregister from load balancer, (2) SIGTERM handler stops accepting new connections, (3) drain in-flight requests with a timeout, (4) close database/Redis connections, (5) exit. The terminationGracePeriodSeconds must be longer than the drain timeout.
  • Load balancer integration: Different load balancers have different deregistration behaviors. AWS ALB has a deregistration delay (default 300s — often too long). Configure it to match your drain timeout. For nginx ingress, the upstream server is removed from the pool when the pod is marked as not ready.
  • Rolling deploy strategy: Use maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 with a readiness gate that does not pass until the new pod is fully initialized. This ensures no traffic gap between old and new pods.

Follow-ups

src.name: Your deploy just broke production
src.desc: 3 PM deploy, 3:05 error rates 10x. The next 15 minutes + long-term safety.
src.q: Is problem ko kaise solve karoge? Your deploy just broke production
src.what:
“You deployed at 3 PM. At 3:05 error rates are 10x. It's your change. Walk me through the next 15 minutes, and how you'd make deploys safer long-term.”

Concepts: Rollback first · Incident comms · Expand/contract migrations · Canary rollout · Feature flags · Blameless postmortem

Kya test hota hai: Incident ownership, rollback-first instinct, blameless prevention thinking.
src.why:
• Rollback first, debug later. Never push a "quick fix" on top of a broken deploy.
  • One caveat to mention: DB migrations can make naive rollback dangerous — that's why migrations must be backward compatible (expand → migrate → contract).
src.answer:
First 15 minutes

  • Roll back immediately. Don't debug live, don't push a "quick fix" on top. Restore the last known good version — minutes of downtime is the metric that matters.
  • Communicate: post in the incident channel — what's broken, impact, that you're rolling back, ETA. Silence is the worst move.
  • Verify recovery: error rates back to baseline, key user flows working.
  • Caveat — DB migrations: if the deploy included a migration, naive rollback can break the old code. Migrations must be backward compatible (expand → migrate → contract): add the new column, deploy code handling both, backfill, remove the old column in a later release.

Afterwards

  • Root-cause offline; blameless postmortem: why didn't tests/staging catch it, and which safeguard was missing.

Making deploys safe

  • Canary / staged rollout: ship to 5% of traffic, auto-halt on error-rate spike.
  • Feature flags: decouple deploy from release — turn the feature off without redeploying.
  • Post-deploy smoke tests, one-click rollback, deploy-correlated alerts, small frequent releases over big-bang ones.

Staff+ Analysis

  • Incident response: Staff+ engineers lead with rollback, not debugging. The first action is always restore service — debug after the fire is out. The instinct to "just look at the code real quick" is the most dangerous impulse in an incident. Train the team: rollback is not failure, it is professionalism.
  • Deploy pipeline: The safeguards that prevent this incident (canary, feature flags, auto-halt) should be built into the deploy pipeline, not optional. Every deploy should go through: build → test → staging → canary (5%) → auto-halt on error → full rollout. No manual gates — automation or it didn't happen.
  • Migration safety: The expand/contract pattern is essential for database migrations in a zero-downtime deploy world. Add the new column, deploy code that reads both old and new, backfill, remove the old column in a subsequent release. This makes every migration safe to roll back.
  • Postmortem culture: The postmortem should focus on systemic questions: why did the deploy reach production? Why did monitoring not catch it earlier? Why was the rollback not instantaneous? The person who deployed is never the root cause — the system that allowed the deploy to reach prod is.

Follow-ups
